## 2. Background

## 2.1. Laser induced water breakdown and plasma evolution

When an ultrashort laser beam is focused into a transparent medium, an optical breakdown occurs once the peak power density exceeds the critical value, leading to the plasma formation. Subsequently, the plasma further absorbs energy from the incident laser via the interaction between laser and plasma, resulting in an increase in free electron density. Thermal energy within the plasma induced by the free electrons diffuses into the target material, thus resulting in material removal through melting and vaporization. ## 2.2. LIPMM using still and flowing water

The target material is completely immersed into water during conventional LIPMM, thus leading to a still water layer. The plasma is formed in the still water layer and then brought to contact with the target material to achieve micromachining, as shown in Fig. 1.

As mentioned above, the plasma formation and evolution have a high dependency on the absorbed laser energy, which is directly affected by the travelling distance in water layer. During LIPMM using still water (S-LIPMM) process, the movement of mechanical platform induces water waves, especially at high speed. The instability and discontinuity of water layer lead to the change of the laser intensity, thus resulting in the unstable plasma. Moreover, the focus plane of the plasma changes with the variation of the water layer thickness as well as the unstable plasma. In addition, small air bubbles resulting from the collapse of plasma induced cavitation are consequently generated and adhered to the workpiece, interrupting the laser propagation in water through reflection and refraction. This significantly reduces the laser intensity stability, leading to the variation of the plasma energy, which further affects the micromachining quality.

In this study, in order to improve micromachining quality, LIPMM using flowing water (F-LIPMM) is developed and to provide a stable and thin water layer on the top workpiece surface, as shown in Fig. 2. According to the flow characteristics, the directional water jet from the nozzle creates a stream consisting of three parts, i.e. impact area, steady flow area and turbulent flow area. The steady flow area is adjusted to incorporate with the laser beam, which results in a uniform and stable water layer in the machined region. Thereby, the thickness of water layer can be guaranteed regardless of the movement of the mechanical platform by using the steady flow area. Moreover, as water jet continuously strikes the top surface of the workpiece, the air bubbles induced by plasma can be flushed away by the formed flowing water layer. These characteristics are beneficial to create stable laser beam intensity and plasma, thus improving the ablation stability. Additionally, the flowing water layer can carry away the ablation debris and excessive heat induced by plasma, thereby potentially reducing the size of HAZ and the number of resolidified particles.

## 3. Experimental details

A Nd:YVO4 solid-state laser from Edgewave (PX50) providing 532 nm wavelength and 10 ps pulse duration was used for LIPMM. AISI 304 stainless steel samples with a size of 22mm×22mm×0.8mm were used as the experimental materials. The laser beam was transferred to a 50mm focusing lens through a beam delivery system, and then a spot size of 16 μm was achieved on the focal plane in air. The

picosecond laser, beam delivery system and workpiece were mounted on a 3-axis motion stage with a movement precision of 500 nm. For SLIPMM, the workpiece was firmly adhered to a support, which was mounted on an acrylic container, as shown in Fig. 1. The acrylic container was filled with distilled water, leading to a still water layer with a thickness of ∼1mm above the workpiece. In the case of F-LIPMM, a distilled water jet from a nozzle impacted the workpiece surface to generate a thin water layer with steady flow. The nozzle with a diameter (dw) of 1mm was mounted above the workpiece with an inclination angle of 45°, a stand-off distance (lw) of 28 mm and a water jet offset distance (xw) of 6 mm, as shown in Fig. 2. A flow rate of 330 cm 3 / min was applied to form a stable flowing water layer in the processing area.

During experimentation, plasma was generated near the laser focal point, and was subsequently adjusted to tightly focus on the target surface via the plasma focusing process for S-LIPMM as well as for FLIPMM. More details of the plasma focusing process refer to [13]. Micro-channels were created by consecutive crates resulting from single plasma discharge. Single factor tests were chosen to compare the machining characteristics of S-LIPMM and F-LIPMM and to investigate the influences of laser process parameters on the geometric characteristics, machining stability, HAZ and MMR of the created micro-channels. After some preliminary tests, the frequency ranging from 2 to 18 kHz, scanning speed ranging from 0.5 to 10mm/s and pulse laser energy ranging from 5 to 35 μJ were employed in this study to create micro-channels with a length of 500 μm. The specific experimental data are shown in Table 1. The scanning of laser induced plasma was repeated twice to achieve the micro-channels with a measurable depth.

After LIPMM, the samples were cleaned in an ultrasonic bath by alcohol for 20min and then blown dry. The surface morphologies and geometric characteristics of the micro-channels were observed by a confocal laser scanning microscope from Olympus (OLS-400). The MRR of single scanning was used and calculated based on the transverse cross-section profile combined with the scanning speed. The machining stability was evaluated by a normalized depth profile in the longitudinal direction, which was calculated by subtracting the mean depth from the longitudinal depth and dividing by the mean depth. To reduce measurement errors, each test was repeated five times, recording the mean value as the final result.

## 4.2. Influence of frequency on the created micro-channel

The planar images, 3D images, transverse cross-section profiles and longitudinal depth profiles of typical micro-channels created by SLIPMM and F-LIPMM at a scanning speed of 5mm/s, a pulse energy of 20 μJ and pulse frequencies of 2 and 14 kHz are presented in Fig. 5. Similar to the previous comparison, micro-channels created by FLIPMM have smaller HAZs than those of S-LIPMM for both frequencies of 2 and 14 kHz, as shown in Fig. 5(a), (b) (e) and (f). In addition, the depth of the micro-channel created by F-LIPMM at the pulse frequency of 2 kHz is slightly larger than that of S-LIPMM, as depicted in Fig. 5(c). The two micro-channels are similar in width. However, the depth of the micro-channel created by F-LIPMM at the pulse frequency of 14 kHz is up to 12 μm, which is generally over twice as much as that created by SLIPMM, 5.4 μm, whereas the width in the case of S-LIPMM is bigger than that of F-LIPMM but not much, as depicted in Fig. 5(g). Moreover, as it is evident from Fig. 5(d) and (h), the micro-channels created by FLIPMM have a superior uniformity in their depth profiles.

More details about the micro-channels created by two processes with various frequencies are shown in Fig. 6. As illustrated in Fig. 6(a), the depths of micro-channels processed by S-LIPMM and F-LIPMM both have an obvious increase with the increasing frequency from 2 to 10 kHz, and then present a mild increase with the frequency further increasing to 18 kHz. Moreover, the effect of frequency on the width is illustrated in Fig. 6(b), showing that for both two processes as the frequency increases, the width increases. Fig. 6(c) indicates that the MRR rises fast with the frequency ranging from 2 to 10 kHz and then has a slight increase with the frequency ranging from 10 to 18 kHz. Apparently, the MRRs processed by F-LIPMM are larger than those machined by S-LIPMM, and the biggest gap under the same conditions in this experiment is more than twice.

A micro-channel with a higher aspect ratio can be achieved at a higher overlap, i.e, with a lower scanning speed or a higher frequency [28]. The MRR has a high dependence on the depth and width of the created micro-channel, as well as the scanning speed. Even though a much deeper and wider micro-channel is created at a low scanning speed, the MRR still increases with the increasing scanning speed from 0.5 to 5mm/s. It can be inferred that the scanning speed has a strong impact on the MRR during this period. Then the MRR decreases with the scanning speed increasing from 5 to 10mm/s due to the fact that the size of microchannel contributes more to the MRR than the scanning speed at this period. When the scanning speed is fixed, an increase in the frequency leads to a deeper and wider micro-channel due to the increase of overlap, thus enhancing the MRR.

With the increase of pulse energy in this experiment, the depths of micro-channels created by two LIPMM process both increase at the beginning, and afterwards, have a tendency to become saturated or even decline. As studied by [13], the electron density of the formed plasma increases with an increase in pulse energy from 5 to 25 μJ, leading to a similar enhancement in the machined depth as a result of the increased temperature and thermo-ablation of the material. Meanwhile, the width has a slight growth with the increasing energy owing to the increase of plasma size. It can be inferred that the energy within the plasma is spread more vertically than horizontally in the distilled water. The electron density at the pulse energy of 30 μJ is close to the upper limit value within the plasma. At this high electron density, the plasma turns to highly reflective and the incoming laser light results in an increase of the plasma volume rather than a further growth of the electron density, as reported by [23]. Hence, the machined depth seems to become saturated with the pulse energy varying from 25 to 35 μJ for F-LIPMM. In the case of S-LIPMM, a slight decrease occurs with the pulse energy increasing from 25 to 35 μJ. The fluctuation of water layer and generation of bubbles during S-LIPMM may be responsible for the reduction of the machined depth. The variation of the micro-channel depth and width also contribute to the MRR. Hence, the trends for the dependences of MRR and depth on the pulse energy are similar.

In general, the influences of scanning speed, frequency as well as pulse energy on the machined characteristics of micro-channels between two processes are similar. However, the comparative results also indicate that micro-channels with smaller HAZ, higher aspect ratio, smoother surface and higher MRR can be created by F-LIPMM at the same laser parameters. It is important to point out that a higher scanning speed and higher frequency can be used in F-LIPMM without compromise of the machining quality, which has the potential to improve the machining efficiency. This better performance can be attributed to the introduction of flowing water layer. Firstly, the stability and thickness of the water layer can be guaranteed in spite of shaking caused by the movement of the platform especially at high scanning speed, which results in a stable laser intensity as well as a steady plasma. Moreover, a directional flow can availably carry away the ablation debris and bubbles suspended in water above the processing area, which will reduce the obstruction and interference of solids and bubbles during laser propagation through the water layer, thus in turn maintaining the stability of laser intensity. Additionally, better cooling performance can be reached through the application of flowing water [29]. Hence, excessive heat induced by LIPMM can be taken away effectively over the ablation region in the case of flowing water, thus limiting the size of the HAZ.

## 5. Conclusions

A new LIPMM approach (F-LIPMM) was developed in this research, where the target material was ablated by formed plasmas in a flowing water layer. The influences of scanning speed, frequency and pulse energy on the machined characteristics between S-LIPMM and F-LIPMM were experimentally investigated and compared. The findings can be highlighted as follows:

- (1) Compared to S-LIPMM, F-LIPMM produces a uniform and stable water layer in the machined region. A flowing and stable water layer is beneficial to create stable plasma, and to carry away the ablation debris, bubbles and excessive heat. Hence, at the same laser parameters, F-LIPMM results in machining of micro-channels with smaller HAZ, smoother surface, higher aspect ratio and higher MRR. However, the influences of scanning speed, frequency and pulse energy on the machined characteristics of micro-channels between two processes are similar.
- (2) A decrease in scanning speed or an increase in frequency increases the machined depth and width of the created micro-channels due to the enhancement of the overlap between consecutive plasmas. The effect of overlap on the depth is more pronounced compared with that of the width. The MRR has a high dependence on the depth and width of the created micro-channel, as well as the scanning speed. A high scanning speed and high frequency can be used in F-LIPMM without compromise of the machining quality, which has the potential to improve the machining efficiency.
- (3) The machined depth of the micro-channel increases with an increase in pulse energy. This is because that the electron density of the formed plasma increases with the increasing pulse energy, giving rise to more thermal energy and higher temperature within the plasma. Subsequently, the induced thermal energy transfers into the target material, thus resulting in more material removal via melting and vaporization. Meanwhile, the pulse energy plays a minor role in the variation of the machined width of the microchannel. The effect of the pulse energy on the MRR is similar to that of depth.

## H I G H L I G H T S

- Micro-channels were fabricated on stainless steel samples by using F-LIPMM.
- Multi-objective optimization tests were carried out.
- The developed regression models were found adequate.
- The optimal process parameters of F-LIPMM were obtained.

## A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: Laser induced plasma micromachining Flowing water Micro-channels RSM

## 1. Introduction

Micro-textures have attracted considerable interest in recent years due to the promising potential for tuning wettability [1-5], friction and wear [6-8], reflectively [9,10], adhesion [11,12], to name a few. Among current micromachining technologies, direct laser machining has been widely applied to create designed micro-textures owing to its excellent characteristics like high flexibility, superior dimensional control and tool-less nature. The thermal accumulation induced by long pulse laser machining results in serious recast layers and heat affected zone (HAZ), which would limit the ultimate performance in some applications [13]. Picosecond laser machining can be used to reduce HAZ, however, it is still hard to process materials with high reflectivity or low absorptivity [14]. Femtosecond laser machining suffers from its high price and low material removal rate (MRR) in spite of its strong

## A B S T R A C T

In this study, laser induced plasma micromachining using flowing water (F-LIPMM) was performed to create micro-channels on stainless steel surface. The effects of process parameters (water speed, laser pulse energy, frequency and scanning speed) on the responses of micro-channel width, depth, material removal rate (MRR) and heat affected zone (HAZ) were investigated based on response surface methodology (RSM). The regression models for the machined width, depth, MRR and HAZ were developed, and the adequacies of the developed models were subsequently verified by analysis of variance (ANOVA) method. Finally, grid structures consisting of desired micro-channels were created with the optimum process parameters: water speed of 8m/s, pulse energy of 10.4 μJ, frequency of 15.8 kHz and scanning speed of 2.7mm/s. The uniform micro-channels with smooth bottoms, side-walls and small HAZ were obtained, and the results showed that the predicted responses using the developed models were comparable with the experimental results.

processing capabilities [15]. Laser induced plasma micromachining (LIPMM) has emerged as a promising one to create micro-features because of its outstanding advantages, such as high precision, high aspect ratio, small thermal damage, multi-material capability and so on [16,17]. In LIPMM process, the laser beam is focused on the liquid medium and the plasma is generated once the peak power density of the incident laser exceeds the breakdown threshold value [18,19]. The plasma then interacts with the laser and absorbs energy, which induces a continuous increase in the free electron density, eventually leads to an increase of temperature within the plasma. When the plasma is brought in contact with the target material, the thermal energy inside the plasma spreads into the material, resulting in the material removal through melting and vaporization. Meanwhile, the mechanical energy generated by the plasma causes shock waves and cavitation [20,21], which also contribute to the elimination of the molten and vaporized

In the past decade, a number of studies have been made to investigate the machining capabilities and characteristics of LIPMM. For example, Pallav and Ehmann [17] demonstrated the feasibility of LIPMM through creating micro-channels on the steel and quartz, and showed that LIPMM surmounted the limitations of conventional ultrashort laser micromachining and micro electro-discharge machining (µEDM). In follow-up studies, Pallav et al. [22,23] systematically compared the capabilities of LIPMM, ultrashort laser micromachining and µ-EDM, and demonstrated that LIPMM could fabricate micro-channels with better performances, like near-vertical walls, uniform profiles, high aspect ratios, small HAZs and high MRRs. Wang et al. [24] used ultrashort laser micromachining and LIPMM to create micro-channels on Al2O3 based ceramic. Comparing with ultrashort laser micromachining, micro-channels with better surface morphologies and high aspect ratios were obtained by using LIPMM. Saxena and Ehmann [25] experimentally demonstrated the multimaterial capability of LIPMM through machining micro-channels on conventional metals, polymers as well as optically transmissive, reflective, and rough surface materials. Meanwhile, several theoretical models about the plasma evolution have been developed to further tap the potential and improve the process of LIPMM. Saxena et al. [26] constructed an axisymmetric model of spatial and temporal distribution of laser induced plasma in distilled water to understand the material removal and machining performance. The influences of pulse energy on LIPMM focusing and machined geometry were investigated by Wang et al. [27] through theoretical simulations and corresponding experimental studies. In order to enhance the productivity of LIPMM, several variant processes have been developed. Malhotra et al. [28] and Saxena et al. [29] used optics to create linear plasma instead of conventional spot shape to improve the machining efficiency. Magnetic field was used to confine the shape of laser induced plasma and to enhance plasma energy density, which in turn improved the machining efficiency [30-32]. Saxena et al. [33] focused a laser beam in an aqueous medium with added salinity and enhanced the energy density of the induced plasma as compared to that generated by distilled water. The result showed that the MRR was improved as high as 97% when creating micro-channels on Aluminum at optimal parameters.

In the above studies, the static water layer was adopted during LIPMM. That is, the workpiece was immersed in the stationary water, and the laser was focused on the water layer above the workpiece to create plasma. Despite the ease use of the equipment, the utilization of static water layer has several disadvantages, which restricts the process of LIPMM. First of all, the rapid movement of the mechanical platform leads to the shaking of the water layer, which induces the variation of the incident laser intensity and makes the formed plasma unstable. Thereby, a low scanning speed is required to ensure the stability of the static water layer. In addition, this process would create a large number of ablative debris and bubbles, which prevent the laser propagation in water. Therefore, a low repetition rate is necessary in LIPMM process to provide plenty time for removing debris and bubbles and for smoothing the processing area before the trigger of next plasma. In LIPMM process, although micro-channels with high aspect ratios are generated, the scanning speed and frequency are quite low, which greatly reduces the machining efficiency. In our previous study, an extension of LIPMM using flowing water (F-LIPMM) was put forward to improve the machining efficiency and to ensure the machining quality [34]. The effect of process parameters (pulse energy, frequency and scanning speed) on the machining characteristics between F-LIPMM and conventional LIPMM were experimentally investigated through single factor test. The result showed that the flowing water layer was beneficial to carry away debris, bubbles and to generate stable plasma. However, the machining process under the coupled effect of laser, flowing water and plasma need to be further investigated and optimized for the high machining efficiency and high surface quality.

Various researchers have employed statistical and analytical

approaches to investigate and to optimize the laser beam machining process. For example, Chen et al. [35,36] designed orthogonal experiments to analyze the effect of process parameters on creating microchannels on polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) and polycarbonate (PC) substrates using CO2 laser, and the optimal machining parameters were obtained through rang analysis. Wang et al. [37] developed mathematical models using Taguchi methodology to study the effect of overlap and overscan number in laser surface texturing of medical needles. They further developed regression and least squares support vector machines (LS-SVM) models to predict the machined depth in laser surface texturing of medical needles [38]. Alahmari et al. [39] construed mathematical models based on response surface methodology (RSM) to study and optimize the fabrication of micro-channels on aerospace alloys. Feng et al. [40] developed quadratic regression models using RSM to investigate and optimize the hybrid laser-waterjet micromachining of single crystal SiC wafers. Another RSM-based modeling and multi-response optimization of the nanosecond laser micromachining of micro-channels on polycrystalline diamonds have been carried out [13]. From the existing literature, experiment-based statistical analysis and models are proved to be effective and convenient approaches to investigate the coupled effect of multi-parameters during laser beam machining and to optimize the process. However, authors could not find any literature related to experiment-based modeling and optimization of LIPMM process. Due to the significant potential, the experiment-based methodology is a promising technique to improve the machining performance of F-LIPMM.

The motivation for this study is to investigate the interactive effect of multi-parameters on the machining performance of F-LIPMM and to provide an insight into the multi-response optimization. Micro-channels (Single-pass) are the fundamental building elements in surface texturing and can be arrayed or joined to form complex patterns and freeform geometries. In this study, F-LIPMM was used to generate microchannels on stainless steel samples. Experiments are conducted based on RSM taking into account of water speed, pulse energy, frequency and scanning speed. Then the regression models of width, depth, MRR and HAZ are established and the effects of process parameters on responses were investigated. Finally, the optimal process parameters of desired micro-channels are obtained and verified.

## 2. Experimental details

## 2.1. Materials and experiment setup

The AISI 304 stainless steel sheets with a thickness of 0.8mm were used as the test samples. F-LIPMM was applied to fabricate microchannels on stainless steel samples, and the setup is illustrated in Fig. 1a. A commercial picosecond laser produced by Edgewave (PX50) was used to generate plasma in distilled water. The pulse duration of the laser is 10 ps and the wavelength is 532 nm. The laser beam with Gaussian profile was focused onto the sample after going through an optical system, producing a spot diameter of ∼16 μm. The laser system was equipped with a 3-axis motion stage, which has a translation precision of 500 nm. A thin and steady flowing distilled water layer was formed on the sample surface by the impact of a waterjet. The waterjet was shot from a nozzle with a diameter (dw) of 1mm, which was positioned above the sample with an offset distance (xw) of 6mm, a shooting distance (lw) of 28mm and a slant angle of 45°, as shown in Fig. 1b. The laser was guaranteed to focus on the steady flow region by using these values.

## 2.2. Experiment design

During F-LIPMM, plasma was produced in the flowing distilled water layer, and was then adjusted to tightly focus on the sample surface through the plasma focusing process, which was achieved by creating multiple parallel micro-channels with various distances of the Optics and Laser Technology 126 (2020) 106067

In order to investigate the effects of process parameters on the machining characteristics and find the optimal values for obtaining desired microchannels with high aspect ratio, high MRR and small HAZ, RSM was used to design the experiments. The screening of F-LIPMM parameters and their levels were conducted based on the literature survey in similar works such as Refs. [22,33,41], as well as on the available facilities, pilot experiments and our previous studies [27,34]. Four predominant factors, i.e., water speed, pulse energy, frequency and scanning speed were selected. The appropriate levels of input factors were selected based on pilot experiments, as shown in Table 1. Using the selected factors (four) and parameters levels (five), an L30 array based on central composite design (CCD) was planned. The responses of interest in F-LIPMM of micro-channels, namely the machined width, depth, MRR and HAZ were selected. Each micro-channel was scanned twice for a relatively large depth.

After F-LIPMM, the samples were cleaned using a 30min ultrasonic bath in alcohol and then dried. A confocal laser scanning microscope produced by Olympus (OLS4100) was utilized to observe the surface morphologies and to measure the geometric dimensions of the microchannels. The geometric dimensions of the transverse cross-section profile combined with the scanning speed were then used to calculate the MRR. Each measurement was repeated five times, and the average value was recorded as the ultimate result.

## 3.4. Experimental validation

To assess the effectiveness of the developed regression models, additional five experiments were performed. For these experiments, the parameter combinations were selected randomly in the range of the models. The experiment results are listed in Table 7. The comparison of the predicted values using the developed models and the experimental results is presented in Fig. 8. As can be seen from the Fig. 8, the developed models predict the width, depth, MRR and HAZ with the average errors of 6.7%, 9.6%, 9.7% and 2.3%, respectively, and the maximum errors of 11.5%, 17.5%, 12.5% and 4.9%, respectively. The errors appear to be acceptable and the models fit and reflect the experimental results well.

Micro-channels with a high aspect ratio have attracted considerable interest and been widely used in diverse applications, such as heat exchanger [48,49], micro-fluid device [50,51], superhydrophobic surface [3] and so on. As a case of study, the creation of a micro-channel with the high aspect ratio, high machining efficiency and excellent surface quality was selected, and the narrow width, high depth, large MRR and small HAZ were expected. The Design-Expert software was used to solve multi-objective optimization [13,40]. The optimization criteria dealt with reaching maximum depth and MRR, minimizing width and HAZ as well, and confining the process parameters within the test range. The obtained optimal parameters for water speed, pulse energy, frequency and scanning speed were 8m/s, 10.4 μJ, 15.8 kHz and 2.7mm/s, respectively. The predicted values of the width, depth, MRR and HAZ were 18.7 μm, 21.5 μm, 32.9×10 4 μm 3 /s and 32 μm, respectively. Grid structures consisting of perpendicular micro-channels were created with the optimal process parameters, as shown in Fig. 9. It is clearly seen that the uniform micro-channels possess smooth bottoms and side-walls with small HAZ, and the actual width, depth, MRR and HAZ are approximately 18.8 μm, 20.8 μm, 30.8×10 4 μm 3 /s and 33.4 μm, respectively. The experimental results are consistence with the predicted values, and the percentage of prediction errors of width, depth, MRR and HAZ are 0.5%, 3.4%, 6.8% and 4.2%, respectively, which are acceptable. The results demonstrate high consistency between the predicted and experimental values. Therefore, the developed models can be used to predict responses and to optimize the process parameters.

## 4. Conclusions

In this study, F-LIPMM was performed to fabricate micro-channels on stainless steel samples. Experimental investigation and optimization of F-LIPMM based on RSM were conducted. The conclusions can be highlighted as follows:

- (1) The developed regression models for the machined width, depth, MRR and HAZ were found adequate, and could be used to predict each response during F-LIPMM.
- (2) The high scanning speed, low pulse energy, high water speed and low frequency were prone to micro-channels with small width. A deep micro-channel was easy to be obtained at low scanning speed, high pulse energy, high water speed and high frequency. With high pulse energy, high water speed, high frequency and low scanning speed, the MRR was relatively high. The low pulse energy, high water speed, high scanning speed and low frequency were

favourable for fabrication of micro-channel with small HAZ.

- (3) The desired micro-channels with high aspect ratio, high machining efficiency and excellent surface quality were created with the optimum process parameters: the water speed of 8m/s, pulse energy of 10.4 μJ, frequency of 15.8 kHz and scanning speed of 2.7mm/s obtained by the multi-objective optimization. The uniform microchannels with smooth bottoms, side-walls and small HAZ were obtained, and the actual width, depth, MRR and HAZ were approximately 18.8 μm, 20.8 μm, 30.8×10 4 μm 3 /s and 33.4 μm, respectively. The percentage of prediction errors were acceptable.

## 2. Materials ablation mechanisms by LIPMD

## 2.1. Processing mechanisms of LIPMD

The LIPMM is a novel process to perform micro-machining. Plasma is induced at the focal point of laser beam in a transparent liquid, as shown in Fig. 1(a). Electrons are generated at the focal point of laser, when the peak power density produced by laser exceeds the threshold value in a dielectric medium, such as deionized water and ethanol. And the evo­ lution equation of free electrons in the dielectric medium can be calculated by the formula (1)[28]:

Where (dρ/dt)mp denotes multiphoton ionization, η casc ρ donates cascade ionization, and η rec ρ 2 denotes recombination. According to formula (1), the shape and intensity of plasma are closely related to free electrons. If the free electron density exceeds the critical value, optical breakdown will be induced in the medium generating a dense and optically opaque plasma at the focal point of laser beam[24,25]. Because the plasma is optically opaque, it absorbs almost all the energy of the incident laser beam[22]. So, the energy of plasma depends on the incident laser beam.

During the process of laser induced plasma micro-drilling, the energy from laser stored in the plasma is transferred to the CFRP material when the plasma interacts with the material of samples. The size of the plasma induced by the laser continues to expand with the increase of repetition frequency, resulting in higher fluence. This is mainly attributed to the fact that the more laser pulses are input, the more electrons acquire the kinetic energy from incoming laser energy, resulting in a larger plasma plume and fluence [29]. A large amount of thermal energy from plasma concentrated on the material of the CFRP resulted in the temperature instantaneous increasing at the interaction of the CFRP, which causes the workpiece material to melt or even vaporize at the point of plasma interaction. The plasma expanding applies a large amount of pressure to the surface of the CFRP samples. The pressure exerted by the plasma suppresses the molten material. The plasma collapses and the dielectric rushes back to fill the void at the end of the laser pulse. The sudden drop in pressure caused by the collapse of the plasma results in the instan­ taneous ejection of molten and vaporized material from the CFRP samples, leading to material removal from the workpiece. When the laser is fed at a certain speed, the plasma is also processed on the surface of the workpiece at a certain feed speed, and the pits on the surface of the workpiece overlap and generate microchannels. The ablated pits are overlapped to generate micro-grooves, and the path of the laser is designed to generate micro-holes[18]. Compared with laser processing, LIPMM machining micro-textures over large areas is more efficient. In addition, this process can achieve a large aspect ratio, while maintaining high processing accuracy[25].

Based on the above LIPMD processing mechanism, the CFRP material is removed based on the thermal and mechanical energy of the plasma. Therefore, the taper of samples machined by the LIPMD process is smaller than that of in the LIA process, and the LIPMD has great advantages in processing micro-structure.

## 3. Experimental procedure

## 3.1. Experimental materials and setup

The CFRP composites plate is used for this investigation with a thickness of 0.3 mm, which is consisted of one twill weave plie. ## 4. Results and discussion

## 4.1. Analyzing quality of micro-holes

The effect of the LIA and LIPMD process on the surface integrity of micro-holes are investigated under the same processing parameters. The surface quality, the diameter of the bottom hole, and the recast layer are both analyzed. From Figs. 6 and 7, it can be obtained that the roundness of bottom holes in the LIPMD is better than that of machined by the LIA. This is mainly contributed to the fact that material is removed by thermal ablation in the LIA process. The epoxy resin on both sides of the kerf is melted by high-temperature. When the processing is completed, melted material is re-solidified to form a recast layer on the processed sidewall, which scatters and refracts the laser reducing the machining stability. Therefore, the material of bottom holes at the local position is not completely removed due to the poor stability of laser. So the roundness of the micro hole is low. However, the LIPMD process pro­ posed in this article is carried out in the ethanol medium, which can not only take away a large amount of thermal but also flush the machined surface reducing the formation of the recast layer. In addition, the me­ chanical energy causes a liquid-gas phase transition, accompanied by cavitation created by the shock wave, which also aids in the removal of molten material within the processing zone[18]. Less recast layer affects processing stability of the LIPMD, so the roundness of bottom holes in the LIPMD is better than that of machined by the LIA process.

In this study, the theoretical diameter of the microhole is 210 μm. While in the experiment, the average diameter of the bottom hole pro­ cessed by LIA is about 167.07 μm, which is less than 20.44% of the theoretical diameter. The average diameter of the bottom hole processed by LIPMD is about 211.1 μm, which is more 0.52% than the theoretical diameter. This may be due to the fact that the molten materials and erosions could not be taken away in time during the processing in the LIA process, and re-solidified on the processed surface, forming an irregular striped side wall. As the processing depth increases, deeper stripes and uneven surfaces are formed, as shown in Fig. 13(1). The uneven surface blocks laser beam and has a scattering effect on the laser. Therefore, the diameter of the bottom hole is smaller than the theoret­ ical value, and the edge is rough with a lot of burrs. In the LIPMD pro­ cess, the liquid medium and liquid-gas phase change takes away erosions, reducing the formation of the epoxy resin recast layer, and the side wall of the micro-holes is close to vertical. So the actual diameter of the bottom hole is close to the theoretical diameter.

The quality of the bottom hole edge processed by the LIA and LIPMD are comparatively analyzed. The edges of the bottom holes in the LIA process are uneven with uncut CFRP material, while the edge of the bottom holes in the LIPMD process is smoother. And the actual diameter of micro-holes in LIPMD is close to the theoretical diameter. This is mainly because the LIPMD process is carried out in ethanol, which takes away the molten epoxy to prevent the recast layer formed, so the surface of the hole edges is smooth. In addition, the effect of auxiliary gas caused by plasma processing and the formation of cavities accompanied by shock waves help to remove the molten material in the processing zoon, effectively avoiding uncut materials.

The influence of the number of scanning and laser frequency on the actual diameter of the micro-hole are analyzed. Fig. 8 shows the rela­ tionship between the theoretical diameter and the number of scanning.

## 4.2. Analyzing taper of micro-holes

The influence of the LIA and LIPMD processes on the taper is investigated. Fig. 10(a) shows the influence of the number of scanning on the taper of the hole when v = 1 mm/s and the laser frequency is 50 kHz. It can be found that the taper of the micro-hole increases with the increasing of the scanning times. This is mainly because the machining width is widened as the number of scanning increased. Therefore, the width of the kerf becomes larger leading to an increase in the diameter of the top hole, as shown in Fig. 8(a). However, the diameter of the bottom hole is almost unchanged with the increase of the number of scanning, as shown in Fig. 8(b). The taper is calculated by the formula (2), so it can be obtained that the taper of the micro-hole increases with the increasing of the laser frequency. Fig. 10(b) shows the effect of laser frequency on the taper of the micro hole when v =1 mm/s and the number of scanningtimes = 35. The taper of the micro hole decreases slightly with the increasing of the laser frequency. This is mainly because the increase of the laser frequency improves material removal and the quality of the processed sidewall, which reduce the blocking of the laser beam by the uneroded material or recast layer. Therefore, laser frequency increasing can improve the machining stability and reduce the taper of the microhole.

0.214, and the taper of the hole in the LIPMD process is about 0.110 to 0.145. Compared with the LIA process, the taper in the LIPMD process is reduced by 32.24%-42.11%. The results show that the taper drilled by the LIA is larger than that drilled by the LIPMD. The main reason is that the LIA process removes CFRP material based on the thermal mechanism between the laser beam and CFRP material. And the molten material is re-solidified to form an irregular recast layer on the processed sidewall, which blocks the laser beam, resulting in a large taper. While micro-hole in the LIPMD process, the molten material is taken away by the liquid medium to prevent the formation of the recast layer, which improves the stability of drilling, thereby reducing the taper significantly.

To further analyze the taper of micro-holes, the cross-sectional pro­ file of micro-holes with a diameter of 210 μm were measured by laser scanning confocal microscope. The micro-hole was measured three times, and the average value was taken as the final taper. When scanning times =45, frequency =50 kHz, the taper in the LIA and LIPMD process are about 0.198 and 0.131 respectively, as presented in Fig. 11. And when scanning times = 35, frequency = 50 kHz, the taper in the LIA and LIPMD process are about 0.202 and 0.106 respectively, as shown in Fig. 12. It can be found that the taper of micro-holes machined by the LIA is larger as compared with the taper in the LIPMD process, and the sidewall is uneven because of covered with recast layer.This further il­ lustrates that when the LIA process is used to drill micro holes, a severe recast layer is formed on the processed sidewall, which affects the laser focusing and machining stability. So the larger taper of microholes is generated. Therefore, the LIPMD process can effectively improve the taper of the micro-holes. By comparing the processed surfaces of microholes in the LIA and LIPMD process, it can be obtained that the processed surface of the micro-holes in the LIPMD process is smoother, and the processed sidewall is close to vertical.

## 4.3. Processed sidewall surface morphology

The effect of different processing technology on the sidewall surface quality under the same processing parameters are analyzed, as shown in Fig. 13. As can be seen from Fig. 13(a), the hole wall surface processed by the LIA has a large number of cavities, and a strip-shaped recast layer can be seen at the entrance of the micro-hole. These defects are caused mainly by the large heat, thermal stress, and auxiliary gas in the laser process, inducing volumetric expansion. So a large number of cavities and stripes are formed. While the LIPMD process is carried out in an ethanol environment in this study. During the processing, the erosion and the molten epoxy resin are taken away by ethanol, which prevents the formation of the recast layer, so the carbon fiber and epoxy resin on the processing surface is visible. In addition, the plasma leads to a liq­ uid-gas phase change and cavitation, which induces shock waves taking away erosion to prevent recast layer forming.

Figs. 13(3) and 13(7), it can be seen that the surface morphologies of fiber obtained by the LIPMD process is smoother than that of machined by the LIA. To further explore the effects of the LIA and LIPMD process on the surface integrity of processed sidewall, the distribution of C and O elements were measured by EDS (energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy). It is found that the C element content in the LIPMD process is more than that of machined by the LIA process. It could be contributed to that carbon fiber is mainly composed of C elements, while the main elements of epoxy resin are C and O elements. The surface of carbon fiber with epoxy resin recast layer has less distribution of C element content, as presented in Fig. 13(4), while the smooth carbon fiber surface has relatively more distribution of C element. Therefore, it can be further concluded that the epoxy resin recast layer of the processed side wall machined by the LIPMD is thinner than that machined by the LIA process.

From Fig. 13(1) we can hardly see the kerf of carbon fiber, because the processed sidewall is almost covered with epoxy resin. But the crosssection of the carbon fiber can be clearly seen, as shown in Fig. 13(5). And the surface of carbon fiber is smooth and almost not covered with epoxy resin, as presented in Fig. 13(8). The cross-section along the radial direction of the carbon fiber can be clearly seen at the bottom of Fig. 13 (5) which is honeycomb-shaped. The LIA process removes material by the high temperature at the laser focus. The energy of laser at the focus follows the Gaussian distribution, and the temperature at the edge of the laser focal point can just melt the epoxy around the entrance of micro­ holes. After cooling, the epoxy is re-solidified to a smooth recast layer on the processed sidewall. As the laser focus moves along the z-axis, the recast layer covering the machined surface affects the laser focusing and ablation of material, resulting in a larger taper.

The cross-section of carbon fiber and epoxy resin can be clearly seen in the LIPMD process, and the machined surface is honeycomb-like, as shown in the bottom of Fig. 13(5). This is mainly because the LIPMD is carried out in a liquid environment, and the liquid will take away a large amount of molten material and reduce the formation of a recast layer on the processed wall. In addition, the shock wave pressure bombardment is generated by the plasma during laser-induced plasma machining [24], which will scour the machined surface and cause the recast layer to fall off. There is almost no epoxy resin recast layer on the processed side­ wall, which reduces the scattering and refraction of the laser, so the taper of the micro-holes in the LIPMD process is smaller than that in the LIA. Furthermore, the structure of carbon fiber and epoxy resin of the sidewall can be clearly seen in the LIPMD process. The CFRP with fiber orientation of 0◦ /90◦ is used in the experiment, as shown in Fig. 3. The upper structure of the sidewall is consisted of 0◦ lay-ups carbon fiber, the machined sidewall is along the axis of the carbon fiber resulting in a laminated structure upper the sidewall. And the lower cross-section is consisted of 90◦ lay-ups carbon fiber, the machined section is along the radial direction of the carbon fiber, resulting in a honeycomb structure lower the sidewall, as shown in Fig. 13(5).

It can be concluded from Figs. 13(1) and 13(5) that the taper of the micro-hole processed by the LIPMD is much smaller than that of the micro-hole in the LIA. It is mainly because the molten epoxy cannot be removed in time to form an irregularly shaped recast layer on the hole wall in the LIA process, which blocks the laser beam resulting in a larger taper. However, the processed side wall machined by the LIPMD process is smooth without recast layer, and less obstruction to the laser beam. So the taper of the micro-hole is smaller than that of the hole drilled by the LIA process. Through the above analysis, the quality of the hole wall in the LIPMD process has been significantly improved.

## 4.4. Comparison with previous studies

A comparison is made between this investigation and similar studies. Few researchers have drilled micro-holes in CFRP plates, and Table 4 presents the investigation of micro-hole drilled by EDM or CNC machining. Teicher et al.[32] carried out experiments on investigating electro discharge machinability. The experiments illustrated that microhole without a detectable HAZ was drilled by EDM applying low discharge currents and open circuit voltages drill hole, but frequently changing electrodes reduced the efficiency. Kumar et al.[6] are excellent in drilling holes in EDM, and they used the process of EDM for the microholes making in the CFRPs with a diameter of 110 μm. Although the micro holes have the characteristics of a high aspect ratio, the edge of the hole is seriously damaged by thermal effect from electrode discharge. Dogrusadik et al.[33] drilled micro-holes by CNC machining center with delamination, burrs, and tool wear.

In this study, the LIPMD process is proposed to drilled micro-holes with characteristics of less thermal damage, low taper, and no recast layer. This is attributed to the plasma induced by laser with high thermal energy on the surface of the CFRP resulting in the temperature instan­ taneous increasing, which causes the workpiece material to melt or even vaporize at the point of plasma interaction. Besides, a large amount of pressure is generated by the plasma expanding and applies to the surface of the CFRP samples. The pressure exerted by the plasma suppresses the molten material. At the end of the laser pulse, the sudden drop in pressure is caused by the collapse of the plasma resulting in the instantaneous ejection of molten and vaporized material from the sur­ face. And the ethanol takes away erosion and heat preventing the recast layer formed. From the Table 4, the bottom of the micro holes can hardly see thermal defects and exposed carbon fiber, and the kerf is smooth and the roundness is excellent. Therefore, micro-holes drilled by the LIPMD process are outstanding in roundness and recast layer.

## 5. Conclusions

This article mainly proposed the LIPMD process to drill CFRP microhole improving the machinability and surface integrity of samples using a 532 nm picosecond pulsed laser, especially to reduce the taper of micro-hole. The surface integrity, taper, and roundness of micro holes were comparatively analyzed, and the quality of the processed surface was investigated. From the results, the following main conclusions can be drawn:

- (1) Compared with the LIA process, LIPMD can effectively improve the roundness and quality of the micro-hole edge. Under the same parameters, the taper of hole in the LIPMD process is reduced by 32.02%-47.44% compared with the LIA process.
- (2) For both LIA and LIPMD processes, increasing the laser frequency or scanning times can largen the diameter of the top hole, which increases the difference between the diameter of the bottom and top holes. The experiment shows that the difference between the diameter of the top hole and the bottom hole is reduced by about 24.83%-32.02% as compared with the LIA process. The actual diameter of the bottom hole differs from the theoretical diameter by only about 0.52% in LIPMD, while the difference in LIA is about 20.44%.
- (3) For the LIPMD process, the structure of epoxy resin and carbon fiber on the processed surface are visible. Based on the analysis of C and O elements by SEM-EDS, it is found that the surface of the carbon fiber is covered with less epoxy resin recast layer than that in LIA process.

## 1. Introduction

Surfaces with special properties have been increasingly adopted to various fields, such as aero engineering, bioengineering, microelec­ tronics, and micromachines. It has been widely accepted that the surface function is related to the microstructures on the surface. Surfaces with diversified functions are common in nature. For example, the lower surface of the lotus leaf is super-hydrophilic underwater due to the tabular and convex lumps modified by many nano grooves on the sur­ face [1]. Fish scales, which are covered with a relatively thin mucus layer and oriented micro papillae, exhibit oleophilicity and hydrophi­ licity in the air but superoleophobicity in water [2]. The seaweed surface contained plenty of intrinsic hydrophilic natural polysaccharides, such as alginate, carrageenan, and abundant porous structures [3]. Hence, it

## A B S T R A C T

In this study, a novel coaxial water assisted laser-induced plasma micromachining (CW-LIPM) method was studied to process microstructures on the workpiece surface. In CW-LIPM, a pulsed laser beam with a wavelength 532 nm was focused within a coaxial water jet, leading to the optical breakdown and the subsequent formation of the localized plasma plume. Compared with conventional laser processing, a cleaner surface could be acquired by CW-LIPM, while maintaining the machining resolution and processing accuracy. The mechanism of CW-LIPM and the effects of microbubble explosions on the surface roughness of the workpiece in proximity to the entrance of the processing area have been studied. With the developed experimental setup, the influence of single laser pulse energy, pulse repetition frequency, and water-jet velocity on the plasma distribution was also researched. Moreover, the effects of waterjet speed on the distribution of cavitation bubbles and the relative position on the machining quality of the processed microchannels were also studied, considering the explosions of the micro cavitation bubbles near the workpiece surface due to the pressure difference. Compared with laser micromachining in the air, CW-LIPM could process microstructures with no protrusions and better precision. High-quality surface microstructures could be obtained by combining the higher-velocity waterjet, the lower single pulse energy, multiple scanning passes, and the processing positions 2-3 mm down from the plasma center and 4-5 mm above the bottom. The laser-induced plasma distribution was asymmetric, and the lower half plasma was more suitable for precision processing due to its focused shape, which is preferred to enhance the locali­ zation of the proposed CW-LIPM process.

could maintain durable superoleophobicity underwater. The filefish skin is covered by oriented hook-like spines, which brings unique anisotropic oil-wettability to filefish, hence the filefish have directional self-cleaning ability in oil-contaminated water [4]. There are various types of wettable surfaces in creatures, such as the high adhesion of rose petals [5], the anisotropic wettability of rice leaves [6], the directional adhe­ sion of butterfly wings [7], the anti-fogging ability of mosquito eyes [8] and the water collection of the desert beetle [9,10], etc.

Inspired by the creatures in nature, many artificial functional sur­ faces with particular microstructures have been processed. Various techniques have been employed to functionalize the surfaces by pro­ cessing the controlled microstructures. The traditional mechanical micromachining has a higher machining efficiency, but the machining resolution was limited by the smallest tool size (about 10 μm). Also, the tool is easy to wear, and the precision is affected by the tool stiffness [11]. Ultra-precision manufacturing and chemical modification have been widely applied. Zhao et al. [12] obtained the oleophobic surface by the Bosch etching method, on which a millimeter-scale micro-pillar array micro-texture was covered. Furthermore, the vertical pillar side­ walls were covered with a nano-scale wave structure from top to bottom, and then a fluorosilane molecular layer was coated on the surface. Zhang et al. [13] prepared an amphiphobic surface by placing a stainless-steel mesh above the flame of a candle to deposit a thin layer of soot composed of a large number of carbon nanoparticles (30-60 nm), and subsequent chemical surface modification performed by chemical vapor deposition (CVD). Electrochemical method was also used to prepare surfaces with the desired microstructures. Meng et al. [14] processed the micro/nano hierarchical nanostructure by immersing a pure zinc plate in an ethanol solution of perfluorocarboxylic acid (CF3(CF2)8COOH). Srinivasan et al. [15] prayed a mixture of fluorodecyl POSS and PMMA on the substrate, and it displayed hydrophobic and high oleophobic properties. It has been found that the surface microstructure could transit from a corpuscular or spherical microstructure to a beads-onstring structure and finally to bundled fibers by changing the molecu­ lar weight of the polymer and solute concentration. However, producing coatings by chemical methods has disadvantages such as weak interface adhesion, inaccurate control of thickness, lower efficiency, and diffi­ culties in obtaining the thick coatings. Moreover, the durability of the processed microstructures could be deteriorated by physical friction or chemical corrosion.

Energy beam has also been applied to process surface microstruc­ tures. Kwon et al. [16] utilized ultra-violet (UV)-assisted capillary molding in producing a flat nanostructured polymer surface parallel to the bottom of the polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). It has been proven that the ultra-fast pulsed laser is suitable for high-resolution, tool-less surface microstructure processing [17]. Niu et al. [18] fabricated a series of dimple-textured surfaces with different geometrical parameters (area density, diameter, and depth) on the surface of middle carbon steel via a picosecond pulsed laser (15 ps). The results show that the dimple depth is the main factor that has a significant effect on the friction and wear properties. The surfaces textured optimum depths can effectively improve the friction and wear resistance of the surface.

It has been demonstrated that various hydrophobic surfaces with manipulated water adhesion could be made using femtosecond (fs) pulsed lasers [19]. Li et al. [20] applied the femtosecond laser to irra­ diate a nickel plate that was immersed in a sucrose solution, and hier­ archical micro-cone arrays were formed on the surface of the plate in a single step. S. Hammouti et al. [21] explored the influences of the femtosecond laser-induced nanostructured surfaces on the wetting de­ gree of liquid lithium versus temperature. The result displayed that the wettability of laser-treated materials was changed from lithium-philic to lithium-phobic for temperatures beyond 320 ℃-360 ℃, compared with that of untreated material. Carvalho et al. [22] demonstrated that femtosecond laser texturing was suitable for creating tunable microscale surface topography on alumina toughened zirconia ceramics to enhance the biological response. Gao et al. [8] fabricated artificial mosquito compound eyes through soft lithography, but the hydropho­ bicity of the synthetic counterpart was far less than that of real mosquito eyes due to limitations of the processing method. Dai et al. [23] used femtosecond laser processing of four types of chevron pockets of cemented carbides. The results showed that the chevron pattern texture with a particular texture density could decrease the friction of a YT15 cemented carbide surface compared with that of the un-textured speci­ mens. Wang et al. [24] verified the effectiveness of the micro-textures on the friction and cutting characteristics of single-crystal diamond tools. Four types of micro-textures have been generated on the rake face of the diamond tools with the femtosecond laser. Experimental results showed that the cutting forces and friction coefficients of the micro-textured diamond tools were greatly decreased except for concentric circular texture, and the cutting performances of the single-crystal diamond tools were effectively improved. Although the most apparent advantage of femtosecond laser micromachining is that the processed structure could not be thermally affected, it is achieved under carefully controlled machining parameters and rigorous environment. Thus, femtosecond laser ultra-precision machining puts forward higher demands on the control of machining parameters. Moreover, the conflicts between machining efficiency and the cost of laser processing should be addressed.

Laser-induced plasma has been increasingly introduced to process surface microstructures in recent years. Pallav and Ehmann [25] pro­ posed that laser-induced plasma could be used for micromachining and revealed that the plasma could become an effective material removal tool. Laser-induced plasma micromachining (LIPM) is a high-resolution, high-precision, and tool-less processing method. In LIPM, the workpiece is immersed in the transparent static or dynamic liquid, with the beam focusing above the surface of the substrate and breaking down the dielectric to generate a plasma plume. Laser-induced plasma has an extremely high temperature that exceeds the melting and vaporization temperature of the workpiece materials. The mechanism of material removal in this process is the combined effect of the mechanical breakage generated by shock waves propagating radially from the expanding plasma and the thermal vaporization of the material in contact with the plasma. Saxena et al. [26] reported a micro-fabrication process that achieves high material removal rate by utilizing thermal ablation by a laser-induced plasma inside an aqueous medium with added salinity. Compared with laser processing in the air, it could obtain a higher material removal rate and larger aspect ratio while maintaining the resolution and processing accuracy. In practical situations, many specific materials are difficult to direct process by laser ablation due to the optical or other surface characteristics. In contrast, the laser-induced plasma showed excellent manufacturing potential [27]. It has been demonstrated that LIPM could produce micro-textures in a large area with 6 times higher machining efficiency [28]. We also want to add an external magnetic field to the LIPM process to control the plasma, and the results showed excellent processing performance. However, this technology still needs to be further explored [29]. However, in the previous studies, LIPM proceeded in the static water environment, thus the melt and cavitation bubbles in the machining zone could not be expelled effectively. Hence, the processing depth was restricted. Actu­ ally, the flow field has an important influence on the processing effect. Wang et al. [30] employed laser-induced plasma with different two axes of light and a water column for micro-texture preparation, in which a flowing water layer was covered on the workpiece. However, the water layer was very thin, and the suppression of recoil pressure was relatively small. The surface plasma explosion under a high-energy laser would be obvious, similar to laser shock peening. Moreover, the unidirectional water flow made the processed microchannel rough on one side and smooth on the other side.

In this paper, a coaxial waterjet assisted laser-induced plasma micromachining (CW-LIPM) for processing microstructure has been proposed to improve the machining surface quality, the stability of precision processing, and to avoid the protrusion around the machining area. The laser beam was coupled in the flowing water jet column. Highspeed and a large-diameter water column were used to discharge heat, cavitation bubbles and ablated materials out of the processing area. The laser intensity at the laser focal spot could exceed the breakdown threshold of water, thus generating plasma in the water jet. The effects of the typical parameters of the water jet on the geometry of the plasma zone were studied. Influences of the laser single pulse energy on the processing resolution were also studied. The processing mechanism of CW-LIPM has been explored, and the impact of laser parameters, waterjet velocity on machining efficiency, surface quality, and processing accuracy have been studied. Additionally, experiments were conducted to study the effects of the micro cavitation bubble explosions near the machining area entrance.

## 2. Experimental

## 2.1. Experimental setup

The schematic diagram of the experimental setup is shown in Fig. 1. An EdgeWave Nd:YAG laser (InnoSlab IS200-2-G) with a pulse duration of 8 ns and a wavelength of 532 nm was used for producing the plasma. The laser pulse repetition frequency ranged from 1 KHz to 10 KHz. The obtained maximum single laser pulse energy was 5.98 mJ. The laser energy attenuation within the beam delivery system and the water column was measured by an external laser power meter (FL250A-BB-35, OPHIR Photonics). The laser focal spot has a diameter of 50 μm in the air, but was expanded to 80 μm via glass window and water chamber, with the focal length of 160 mm of the focusing lens.

Although the energy absorption coefficient of the optical compo­ nents in the laser beam delivery system was very low, there was a rise in the temperature of reflectors and the window over the course of time, due to the high energy density associated with the beam. Hence, the surface of the optics had multilayer dielectric metal oxide coatings, which can resist higher laser power. The surge tank offered relatively better pressure stability with minimal fluctuation over a wide range of the velocity of the ultra-pure water drawn up from the storage tank by the pump. The workpiece was mounted on a 5-axis motion stage with a translation resolution of 10 μm and rotational resolution of 20′′ .

## 2.2. Materials and measurement

Two CCD systems were employed for observation and positioning. The first one was used to observe and locate the micro-texture on the workpiece, and the second one was perpendicular to the waterjet to observe the distribution of the laser-induced plasma zone. A laser confocal microscope (KEYENCE VK-X200K) was used for measuring the three-dimensional surface topography. The surfaces were also observed with a scanning electron microscopy (SEM, SU5000, Hitachi). The generation and dissipation of the plasma plume in waterjet were observed by an ultra-high-speed camera (XX RapidFrame, Standford Optics). The length and width of the plasma zone were measured by a CCD system. The workpiece of 304 stainless steel with a thickness of 3 mm was processed by CW-LIPM. The laser scanning speed was 10 mm/s. The experimental conditions are shown in Table 1.

## 3. Characterization of laser-induced plasma distribution in waterjet

## 3.1. Influence of single laser pulse energy on plasma distribution

By changing the laser pump current ranging from 46 A to 60 A, the corresponding single laser pulse energy has been shown in Table 2. The laser pulse repetition frequency was 8 KHz, and the water-jet speed was 2.79 m/s. Both the length and width of the laser-induced plasma zone increased with the increasing of the single laser pulse energy (Fig. 2), as the volume of the plasma magnified with the increase of the laser single pulse energy (Fig. 3). The plasma generally exhibited a fusiform-shaped characteristic. It was also found that with the growth of the laser single pulse energy, the distance between the plasma volume and the nozzle decreased, as illustrated in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4. With the improvement of the single laser pulse energy, the liquid breakdown effect could be more obvious, and the area of the plasma zone increased. The position of the laser beam (surface A in Fig. 5), whose energy density just reached the breakdown threshold of water, moved upward, with the increase of the single laser pulse energy.

As shown in Fig. 5, the laser-induced plasma plume in the water jet exhibits a fusiform shape. When the laser beam propagated downwards within the waterjet, the energy density of the cross-section A first reached the breakdown threshold of water, and thus plasma emerged. As the laser beam traveled downwards before the beam waist, the laser energy density increased. Hence, the plasma volume expanded radially from its top to the center, and the plasma plume at the focal point was the largest and brightest. Due to the existence of the beam divergence angle, when the beam continued to travel through the focal point, the cross-sectional energy density value decreased as the beam transmitted downwards, so less and less plasma was excited. In fact, there was al­ ways the laser running through the plasma volume.

## 3.2. Influence of laser pulse repetition frequency on plasma distribution

Within the laser pulse duration, the high-temperature and highpressure laser-induced plasma absorbed energy continuously, and simultaneously the plasma expanded, pushing the surrounding liquid to expand radially outward. The eclipse time of plasma was on the order of a few microseconds(μs) [31]. The existence time of cavitation bubbles induced by strong laser ranges from hundreds of microseconds to tens of milliseconds. Therefore, the bubbles generated by the previous pulse have not entirely dissipated, and then new bubbles have been generated after the next pulse.

<!-- image -->

The plasma plume emitted strong bright light, and part of light was reflected in the water column, as shown in Fig. 6a. The intense laser could produce cavitation bubbles after breaking down the water, and these bubbles could generate radial shock waves when they collapsed and expanded. As schematically illustrated in Fig. 6b, the plasma in the central area of the liquid column would continuously produce cavitation bubbles. The shock waves generated then pushed the long-lived bubbles to move radially. At the periphery of the jet, these bubbles then exploded due to the sharp decrease in pressure, the water was sputtered.

Fig. 7 shows that the laser pulse repetition frequency changes have no effect on the length of the laser-induced plasma zone. The volume and position of the plasma were only determined by the energy value of a single laser pulse. Thus, the laser-induced plasma plume distribution could only be controlled, to some extent, by adjusting the single laser pulse energy. However, the changing laser pulse repetition frequency influences on the generation of bubbles. The more pulses received per unit time, and the more energy could be utilized to excite the plasma, leading to an increase in the number of micro cavitation bubbles. The cavitation bubbles could affect the substrate material removal, and the shock waves generated when the cavitation bubbles exploded disturbed the residual plasma plume. Hence, the varying frequency could exert an influence on the manufacturing process, which would be discussed later in this paper.

## 4. Results and discussion

## 4.1. Influences of relative position between plasma zone and workpiece

As shown in Fig. 8a, the beginning of the plasma zone was defined as the 0 position. Microchannels were processed by changing the relative position between the plasma zone and workpiece surface. Fig. 8(b) shows the processed microchannels at the corresponding position. In experiments, the workpiece was moved down from the top of the plasma volume vertically by 1 mm in one step to process the parallel micro­ channels. After processing, the workpiece was ultrasonically cleaned in deionized water. The three-dimensional profiles of machined channels were measured by a laser microscopy.

As shown in Fig. 9, in the upper half of the plasma volume (0-14 mm), the processed micro channel became shallower with the workpiece moving downward. However, in the lower half of the relative position, the slot-depth curve increased amid severe fluctuations. In contrast, the slot-width curve dropped gently. This characteristic corresponded to the observed appearance of the fusiform plasma volume. Additionally, the material removal partly was attributed to the laser processing effect, as the laser beam could transmit through plasma volume. When the laser propagated below the focal point, a part of the laser energy has already been used to excite the upper half of the plasma. Thus, the laser energy contained in the lower half plasma volume was less, and the removal of material was more due to plasma ablation. The whole energy of the upper part of the volume was greater than that of the lower part. Therefore, the upper plasma's ability to ablate material was more potent than that of the lower half. If the processing position was not far from the

This combined ablation effect contributed to the deeper channel whose depth was 13.62 μm, manufactured at a distance of 3 mm from the top, and its width was up to 195.39 μm.

In the upper half of the plasma, from its top to the center, laser en­ ergy kept falling and plasma energy kept rising, but the whole energy value declined and the volume cross-section area kept rising, thus the overall energy density decreased, and the energy of the plasma was distributed more sparsely across the cross-section and channels became narrower and shallower. Although the energy density was declining due to the expansion effect, the width of the microchannels within the processing position ranging from � 10 to � 12 mm still maintained a relatively high level. It is worth noting that the diameter of the center of the plasma reached the maximum value, thus the groove width curve displays a "platform" shape at this stage. In addition, the total energy density value was the smallest at this position, so the groove depth here was maintained at the lowest level. In the lower half, both laser energy and plasma energy decreased along the breakdown zone downward, while the cross-sectional area was also falling. I speculated that from the center of the plasma volume down to 1-2 mm above the end, energy density was increasing, and the energy was concentrated. This is in line with the trend of the curve in Fig. 9. The microgrooves processed in this area could be smaller and deeper.

In terms of surface roughness, due to the larger coupling energy and the upper expanded plasma volume, surfaces near channel edges were relatively rough. On the contrary, when we utilized the lower plasma plume, the surfaces were smoother because of the concentrated energy and the faster jet, which would be further explained below. It is worth noting that the volume was not strictly geometrically symmetric.

Considering every aspect under these parameters, the best etching po­ sition was about 4 mm up from the bottom, where we can acquire the highest material removal rate and precision. Also, the channel width under this condition was around 100 μm. Thus, the position 2-3 mm below the center of the plasma zone was preferred for micromachining.

## 4.2. Influences of laser pulse repetition frequency

As shown in Fig. 10a, when the scanning speed remained constant, the higher frequency meant the workpiece per unit time could receive more pulses, thus the slot could be wider. However, as the single pulse energy rose, the volume of cavitation bubbles would also be larger.

As shown in Fig. 10b, when the energy of a single pulse grew, the trend of depth along with the changing frequency was also different: When the energy of a single pulse was 1.34 mJ, the increasing trend of depth at high frequency was milder than that at low frequency. The depth value has slowly decreased since the beginning. This phenomenon suggested that as the amount of removal material augmented, there was a bottleneck effect as the overlap rate rose. Due to the cavitation bubbles generated in liquid, this bottleneck effect was more prominent and forward along with the growing single pulse energy. Either the volume of cavitation bubbles and plasma plume excited by small pulse energy was small, or the distance between two adjacent pulses was large enough, the influence of micro cavitation bubbles on the beam could be ignored, otherwise the bubbles generated by the previous pulse would absorb, refract and reflect the next laser pulse.

## 4.3. Influences of waterjet velocity

As shown in Fig. 11, the higher jet velocity meant the finer surface around the CW-LIPM affected area. Under the experimental conditions, when the jet velocity reached 5.55 m/s, the cavitation pits were no longer visible. However, the jet velocity cannot be increased indefinitely because the buffer capacity of the surge tank could decline with the increment of water pressure. The water could maintain the laminar state within a certain range of waterjet velocity. If the fluctuation range was too extensive, the water jet appeared turbulence, which damaged the stability of CW-LIPM, and resulted in the uneven distribution of the impact pressure towards the processing area, ultimately reduced the machining quality.

The material removal mechanism of CW-LIPM has been clearly shown in Fig. 12a, and the actual processing area of high-speed photography has been shown in Fig. 12c. When the excited plasma touched the workpiece, the ablation pits quickly formed under high temperature. With the movement of the workpiece in lateral directions, microchannels could be processed by CW-LIPM. In the LIPM process underwater, cavitation and vaporization bubbles could be generated by the effect of laser-induced plasma in the liquid environment in the machining area. Hence, the ablated materials, cavitation bubbles and plasma/vapor plume could be pushed out of the machining area by the recoil pressure. In CW-LIPM, with the aid of the high-speed waterjet flow, the expelled ablation material and micro cavitation bubbles could be flushed away. Some cavitation bubbles that were adhered to the workpiece surface exploded after being washed out due to the pressure difference, forming different sizes of cavitation pits around the machining area. Meanwhile, with a larger speed of the waterjet, the ablated materials, cavitation bubbles, and plasma could be washed out more efficiently, and the existence time of the micro-bubbles were shortened. If the flow were fast enough, the bubbles would be flushed away before the explosion, thus smooth processing surfaces could be obtained.

It was also found that during the interval time between two adjacent

When the cavitation bubbles left the machining area, some of them broke suddenly during its compression and rebound, inducing huge collapse pressure compressing the surrounding liquid medium to form a shock wave disturbing the floating plasma plume, and then the waves propagated in liquid. During the final stage of a bubble breakdown, a high-speed jet formed toward the wall. Fig. 12d is the photography of the remaining plasma plume. A high-speed camera was employed to capture the motion of the plumes and the interval between each frame of the video recorded by the highspeed camera was approximately 4.55 microseconds. A video doc­ umenting the entire process of plasma annihilation has been provided. It has been found that during the laser-induced plasma annihilation pro­ cess, the plasmoid flickered, accompanying its volume expansion and contraction. Hence its brightness and size showed a pulsatile attenuation characteristic. The time of the whole annihilation process was about 0.6 ~ 0.9 ms. Because the plasma existed for a too short time, the velocity vector of the flow field did not affect the distribution of the plasma plume, but the waterjet played a significant role in flushing heat, ablated materials, and cavitation bubbles from the deep processing area. How­ ever, more detailed physical processes require further research in the following studies.

## 4.4. Influences of the single laser pulse energy

As shown in Figs. 13 and 14, the increase of the single laser pulse energy would enlarge the microchannels, in which both the depth and width of the microchannels were increased. With a higher laser in­ tensity, the plasma micromachining efficiency could be improved because the size of the laser-induced plasma would be larger, and the time of residual plasma was also extended. However, the improvement in material removal rate did not mean better processing quality. Unlike the micro pits caused by cavitation bubbles, the drifting residual plasma plume existing for a longer time could damage edges of the micro­ channels and deteriorate the surface quality, as shown in Fig. 13. The affected zones were formed due to the diffraction effect of the laser beam caused by plasmons and cavitation bubbles. Therefore, in order to obtain high-quality surface micro-texture via small single-pulse laser energy and the multiple scanning machining methods were recommended.
