## 4.5. Comparison between CW-LIPM and laser micromachining in the air

Fig. 15 shows the microchannels processed by CW-LIPM and laser micromachining in the air, respectively. In CW-LIPM process, the water jet with a velocity of 5.55 m/s, the single laser pulse energy of 4.98 mJ, the pulse repetition frequency of 1 KHz, and the processing position of � 20 mm were used.

With the same laser density, a protrusion was clearly formed at the entrance of the microchannels processed by laser machining in the air, as shown in Fig. 15(a)-(c). Whereas the edge of the channels processed by CW-LIPM, shown in Fig. 15(d)-(f), was very elegant and clean. In laser machining in the air, the protrusion was generated at the entrance of the laser micromachining area due to the accumulation of melt, while the microgrooves made by CW-LIPM are very uniform and neat, without any bumps. With a high-speed waterjet, the ablated material generated in the plasma machining area was washed away, thus, there were no protrusions at the entrance of the micro-channels. Moreover, the cavitation and vaporization bubbles' explosions prevented the melt's adherence on the sidewalls and inlets of the processed microchannels, and also could avoid the recast layer. Fig. 16 shows the surface microtexture processed by CW-LIPM. Additionally, with the combined ef­ fects of the radiation energy of the laser and the energy intensity dis­ tribution of the plasma on the surface of the workpiece, a taper angle of a microstructure processed by CW-LIPM was formed.

The edges of the micro-grooves of the surface micro-texture pro­ cessed by the laser in the air, as illustrated in Fig. 15(a), had defects such as protrusions, burrs and thick recast layers, which were harmful in the oil lubrication and drag reduction, and the secondary processing was required. Contrarily, as shown in Fig. 15(d), the micro-grooves pro­ cessed by CW-LIPM exhibited a different morphology. The morphology has no sharp peaks and was round and smooth, and it was very beneficial for friction reduction. This was obviously caused by the ablation of the substrate by the flowing plasma plume.

Fig. 17(d) is a detailed view of a micro-channel processed by CWLIPM. It could be seen that there were continuous micro pits at the bottom of a channel, which was presumed to be due to the pulsed laserinduced plasma. As shown in Fig. 17(b), there were no micro-pits at the bottom of the microchannels processed by laser machining in the air. The microchannel bottom pits hold the potential to enhance the highpressure oil lubrication. The lubricating oil stored in the pit could maintain the continuity of the oil film under extreme conditions, avoiding and delaying solid-solid contact/dry friction. The initial im­ purities or wear debris could sink to the concave bottom first, delaying malignant scratches and extending bearing life.

## 5. Conclusion

This paper studied coaxial waterjet Laser-induced plasma micro­ machining (CW-LIPM) to process surface microstructure. Experiments were conducted to study the performance of CW-LIPM, considering the effects of the laser-induced plasma position, waterjet velocity, laser pulse repetition frequency and single laser pulse energy. The key con­ clusions of this study are as follows:

1. In the CW-LIPM process, the material removal mechanisms were based on plasma ablation in the front gap. In the lateral machining side gap, the materials are dominantly removed by plasma-induced recoil pressure and explosions of cavitation bubbles, which could guarantee the high machining quality.
2. The mechanisms of CW-LIPM were confirmed by comparison with the laser micromachining in the air. The utilization of a coaxial waterjet could enhance the transfer of the accumulated heat in the substrate near machining gaps. CW-LIPM could improve the machining quality compared with that by laser micromachining in the air. Results showed no protrusions at the machining area entrance, and better geometric accuracy could be obtained.
3. Due to the presence of micro cavitation bubbles, the increasing trend of material removal rate was inhibited. The roughness of the surfaces near machining areas increased, attributed to the shock of microjet followed by the explosions of the micro cavitation bubbles. However, a moderate number of bubbles could make the heat-affected zone
4. thinner and improve the quality of the inner walls of the micro­ structures. When the water velocity was above 5.55 m/s, no micro pits could be observed.
4. During the laser pulse-off period, the remaining plasma plume flickered, and its volume expanded and contracted alternately. The duration time ranged from 0.6 ms to 0.9 ms, as measured by a 220 Kfps ultrafast camera.
5. A comparison of the effects of various machining parameters shows that the machining precision could be improved by using the lower single laser pulse energy, the higher water jet velocity, multiple scanning, and the processing positions 2-3 mm down from the plasma center and 4-5 mm above the bottom. The laser-induced plasma was asymmetric and the lower half plasma was more suit­ able for precision processing due to its focused shape.

llm_description.summary: The study investigates coaxial waterjet assisted laser-induced plasma micromachining (CW-LIPM) for enhancing surface microstructure quality. It highlights the influence of laser parameters and waterjet velocity on machining efficiency and surface quality, demonstrating that CW-LIPM can achieve high precision without protrusions.
llm_description.mechanism: The CW-LIPM process generates plasma in a water jet, utilizing the combined effects of mechanical breakage from shock waves and thermal vaporization for material removal.
llm_description.evidence_quote: High-quality surface microstructures could be obtained by combining the higher-velocity waterjet, the lower single pulse energy, multiple scanning passes, and the processing positions 2-3 mm down from the plasma center and 4-5 mm above the bottom.

## Abstract

Laser Induced Plasma Micromachining (LIPMM) is a novel, tool-less micromachining process which offers machining characteristics superior to conventional laser ablation, such as multi-material capability, higher machined depth and better wall geometries. This study utilizes highly empirical methods for the purpose of a proof of concept and demonstrates the viability of using external magnetic fields in modifying the geometry and improving the aspect ratio of machined spots (up to 6) in LIPMM, which is accomplished by pulling the plasma spatially downward to machine spots with greater depth and consistent diameters, and to achieve horizontal squeezing of the plasma to create channels.

Keywords: Laser Induced Plasma Micromachining; Laser ablation; Magnetically controlled plasma

Laser-induced plasma micromachining (LIPMM) is a relatively new method of micro-manufacturing that utilizes the plasma generated in a dielectric to physically interact with a workpiece. LIPMM has demonstrated its ability to machine a variety of materials such as ceramics, metals, polymers and materials with special surface characteristics such as transparency and high reflectivity [1,2]. However, one of the potential advantages of LIPMM which has remained unexplored is the capability to manipulate plasma plume spatially using an external magnetic field, in order to add more flexibility to the process in terms of produced feature geometry and higher aspect ratios which would otherwise be impossible to achieve using regular LIPMM. This paper explores the method of magnetically-controlled LIPMM (MC-LIPMM) with the aim of producing higher aspect-ratio micro-features and modified feature geometries. Table 1 lists several of the advantages

MC-LIPMM has over more conventional methods, including spot-based LIPMM [3-8].

During plasma generation, dielectric breakdown occurs inside the dielectric media, which may be distilled water, kerosene, mineral oil or another transparent dielectric liquid. Fig. 1 shows an example of plasma generated in a dielectric. When the peak irradiance of the ultra-short pulsed laser beam is greater than the dielectric ionization threshold potential, there is a generation of free electrons leading to the formation of a highly localized plasma zone through optical breakdown of the dielectric [9-11]. The laser induced plasma is then brought in physical contact with the workpiece, which results in vaporization of the material near surface. A key difference with this machining from others is that the mechanical energy in the plasma gives rise to shock waves and cavitation, replacing the dielectric and applying pressure to the workpiece. At the end of the pulse, the dielectric fills back into the void and flushes the debris off the surface of the workpiece, thereby facilitating material removal [12].

The question of feasibility of MC-LIPMM [13] arises from analyses of the effects of magnetically-controlled micro-EDM, which shows that an external magnetic field led to relatively higher debris transportation and helped with flushing during micro-machining of micro-features such as deep channels and holes [14]. Magnetic fields can change the shape of plasma; plasma expands along the direction of magnetic force and compresses in the direction normal to the force. In addition, a surrounding magnetic field can increase oscillating frequency of the plasma and therefore, increase its temperature and energy density [15]. The spatial position of plasma relative to the surrounding magnetic field is a crucial parameter. This study observes the plasma and machining characteristics as a result of various magnetic field configurations around the plasma plume. In addition to observing plasma behavior, more specific objectives include maximizing the aspect ratio of machined spots from the plasma; that is, to move the plasma downward to machine spots with more depth and with consistent diameters, and to achieve maximum squeezing of plasma to create machined channels on the workpiece.

## 1. Material and methods

The laser system used in this study is a commercial (RAPID PS, Lumera) Nd-YVO4 solid-state ultra-short pulsed laser that emits linearly polarized laser pulses of 8 ps pulse duration, at 532 nm wavelength (second harmonic). The beam is redirected to a substrate through a beam delivery system, which consists of a 5- beam expander and a diffraction limited focusing lens of 25 mm focal length. The beam has a Gaussian (TEM00) profile at laser exit. The workpiece is mounted on a positioning system, attached to the laser system. The layout of the laser and positioning systems are in Fig. 2.

Four different configurations of substrate and magnetic field combinations were tested in addition to machining without an external magnetic field, as shown in Table 1. Polyamide (PA 66) and Aluminum Alloy AA5052 were used as substrates. Kerosene or distilled water were used as dielectric media for each setup. At the focal point of the laser, the plasma is in physical contact with the work piece, resulting in the vaporization of the material. At this point for each setup, the shutter of the system opened and the laser-induced plasma machined the substrate for five seconds, and the plasma plume was translated down (into the substrate) by 30 lm at a feed rate of 5 lm/s. Subsequently, the shutter was opened to translate the plasma about 200 lm in either the x or y direction. All experiments were completed with a pulse repetition frequency of 10 kHz and average beam power of 0.13W. Measurements and surface visualization were carried out with an ALICONA Infinite Focus-Optical 3D white light interferometer with 50 nm resolution, as well as with an optical microscope.

A pattern of channel-like plasma machining (L-LIPMM) to spot-like machining (S-LIPMM) could be observed with a variety of the empirical setups, as seen in Fig. 4. Fig. 4 corresponds to configuration (b), with 12 neodymium magnets and kerosene dielectric where elliptic craters were machined 250 lm apart with the left-most crater 750 lm away from the surface of the magnet. Only heat affected zones (HAZ) and no machining were observed with laser-induced plasma without an external magnetic field at the same settings and focal point as the trials with external magnetic fields.

Some factors to keep in consideration include the temperature threshold of the rare earth magnets. Above certain temperatures, the permanent magnets may lose a fraction of their magnetic strength. However, a key factor in MCLIPMM is the amount of control in steadying the magnetic fields surrounding the workpiece and comparing the topology and machining characteristics of resulting channels and spots to those machined without external fields. There is a large amount of variability with the strength of the magnetic field, which is largely dependent on the location of plasma relative to the field and the feed rate of the plasma during machining. More control in the location of the plasma as well as the laser beam relative to the different areas of surrounding magnetic fields can lead to more informed machining and improved aspect ratios. Testing with electromagnets and repeated trials can possibly alleviate the control issue.

## 3. Conclusions

Preliminary results of the MC-LIPMM process show that larger external magnetic fields relative to the region of machining can squeeze or stretch the plasma, leading to channels and spots with larger aspect ratios compared to LIPMM without external magnetic fields. Suggested future work includes multiple trials with a larger variety of magnet setups and configurations, including electromagnets, substrate materials and controls to help fulfill this proof of concept. Model formulation and optimization methods to control and test specific parameters such as field strength, frequency and power of the laser and feed rate are necessary for more predictable and efficient LIPMM process. In-situ manipulation of the process can ultimately lead to complex surface texture geometries and faster machining times.

## 1. Introduction

Laser-induced plasma micro machining (LIPMM) is a new micromachining method proposed by Pallav and Ehmann that has the po­ tential for multi-material processing [1], generation of complex features and high precision microstructure processing. In LIPMM, ultrashort laser pulses are focused in an auxiliary dielectric layer, e.g., water, above the immersed workpiece surface, instead on the original workpiece surface, causing optical breakdown that results in a local plasma plume leading to material removal. The material removal mechanism consists of the combined effect of the thermal vaporization by plasma-material inter­ action, and the mechanical erosion by shock waves from micro bubble

## A B S T R A C T

Magnetically Controlled Laser-induced Plasma Micro-Machining (MC-LIPMM), compared to traditional direct laser ablation, has the ability of achieving better machining characteristics including larger aspect ratios of machined features, a smaller heat affected zone and more diverse micro-structures. To reveal the process mechanisms affected by the magnetic field, this paper studies the evolution and distribution of plasma in MCLIPMM by analytical and experimental methods. An analysis of the confinement effect and enhanced collision of electrons-ions in the plasma in the presence of a magnetic field is performed for revealing the influence of the magnetic field on its diffusion and geometric size. To validate our theoretical predictions, experiments were conducted to analyze the effects of key process parameters on the geometrical size, shape and fluence of the plasma. Edge contour extracting and elliptic formula fitting algorithms were applied for quantitatively evalu­ ating the changes. The experimental results show that transverse magnetic fields generate a larger plasma plume and change its shape from spherical to ellipsoidal compared to that without a magnetic field. The eccentricity of the ellipsoidal plasma exhibits a parabolic growth while the cross-sectional area of the fitted ellipse shows a linear growth as the transverse magnetic field strength increases. Greater growth in geometric size and intensity of the plasma was obtained under a longitudinal compared to a transverse magnetic field, and its shape changed into an elongated ellipsoid. Moreover, a two-dimensional magnetic field, combining both the transverse and the longitudinal magnetic field component, was shown to produce a larger area and intensity of spherical plasma under an appropriate transverse and longitudinal magnetic field strength compared to that without a magnetic field.

formation and collapse. Therefore, the evolution of the plasma plume in the machining process is the key to reveal the material removal mech­ anisms in LIPMM, where, specifically, the shape and intensity of the plasma play a dominant role affecting machining efficiency, quality and the geometric characteristics of the machined micro-features.

To confine the plasma and control its shape, magnetic field assisted technology is proposed due to its significant effect on the size and flu­ ence of the plasma [2]. Pisarczyk et al. applied external magnetic fields to generate elongated plasma columns [3]. They also obtained a higher electron density of the plasma in the presence of the magnetic field. VanZeeland and Gekelman analyzed the expansion of an ambient magnetized plasma induced by a dense laser through experimental methods [4]. In order to reduce energy consumption and thermal deformation in wire electric discharge machining (WEDM), Zhang et al. introduced an external magnetic field to obtain more stable discharges (i.e., plasma) [5]. Begimkulov et al. investigated the evolution of laserinduced plasma in a transverse magnetic field and reported that the dimension of the radial plasma can be increased [6]. Liu et al. explored the influence of magnetic field strength on laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) at various pressures by experimental methods, and found that not only the plasma intensity of the optical emission and its persistence time were boosted with an increase of magnetic strength, but also the plasma plume was separated into two lobes in the presence of the magnetic field [7]. Behera et al. utilized fast imaging technology to observe the dynamical behavior of aluminum plasma induced by laser across 0.45 T magnetic field at low ambient pressure, and it was observed that expanding plume experiences resistive force and ap­ proaches the stagnation limit [8]. Rai et al. observed the optical emis­ sion from laser-induced plasma of liquid samples with and without a magnetic field and confirmed that the enhancement in emission in­ tensity was due to the magnetic confinement effect [9]. Hence, external magnetic field assisted methods can also be effective in changing and controlling the shape, size and fluence of the plasma in LIPMM.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The effects of magnetic fields on machining characteristics in LIPMM were recently explored through experiments. Saxena et al. applied an external unidirectional magnetic field in LIPMM [10], and larger plasma energy (increase by 70%) and deeper micro-features (increase by 50%) were obtained in a magnetic field of 5400 G. Tang et al. utilized the repulsive magnetically controlled LIPMM to fabricate high-quality sur­ face microstructures [11]. Their experimental results showed that a smaller recast layer, heat affected zone and width of micro-groves can be obtained. However, few research works focus on the plasma evolution in real time under different magnetic fields by experimental methods to directly reveal the machining mechanisms in MC-LIPMM. The evolution of the plasma plume in the presence of a magnetic field can be also helpful to control the dynamic properties, geometric shape and size of the plasma, which are essential in plasma-based machining research and fundamental studies.

For the sake of the above research problems, this paper explores the effect of different magnetic fields on the plasma characteristics including its shape, size and fluence. Section 2 presents the mechanism of plasma confinement and collision of electrons-ions in the presence of magnetic fields. The experimental procedures including setup, design and mea­ surement method are described in Section 3. To quantitatively investi­ gate the effects of different magnetic fields on the shape, size and fluence of the plasma, the experimental results and discussion are given in Section 4. Conclusions are drawn in Section 5.

## 2. Background

The aim of this section is to reveal the influence mechanisms of magnetic fields on the evolution and distribution of plasma, the plasma diffusion process, and the variation of collision of electrons-ions in the presence of magnetic fields.

## 2.1. Plasma diffusion in the presence of magnetic fields

The motion trajectory of an electron inside the plasma in the pres­ ence of a magnetic field changes into spiral motion around the magnetic field line due to the Lorentz force, and its gyration radius is defined by the Larmor radius rL. In this paper, the plasma is kind of fully ionized by the laser. We consider the case where the neutral mean-free path for charge-exchange collisions, is quite short compared to the plasma size. As described by Goldston et al. [12], the plasma becomes almost fully ionized at electron temperatures above about 1 eV. Thus, the case of collisions with neutrons is not of much concern to the physicist inter­ ested in high-temperature plasmas. Not only are high-temperature plasmas almost fully ionized, but the dynamical behavior of charged particles even in partially ionized plasmas with more than very small ionization levels tends to be dominated by Coulomb collisions with other charged particles, rather than by collisions with neutrons [8]. Thus, the electron-neutral collision frequency is not considered in our paper. Moreover, since the classical diffusion coefficient is due to plasma re­ sistivity, it arises from electron-ion collisions, and not from electronelectron nor ion-ion collisions [12].

The diffusion of an electron due to collisions with other particles in the presence of a magnetic field is shown in Fig. 1. When an electron collides with other particles, its motion direction changes by a small angle and continues to gyrate along the magnetic field with a changed gyration center. If the collision frequency is much lower than the gy­ ration frequency, the gyration center will undergo a random-walk pro­ cess with a step size equal to the Larmor radius rL. The diffusion coefficient of the plasma can be represented by the diffusion coefficient of the electron [13] and the plasma can be confined by the magnetic field in the direction perpendicular to magnetic field lines.

Coulomb collisions dominate over other collisions in affecting the diffusion in a fully ionized plasma. The classical diffusion in a fully ionized plasma is intrinsically ambipolar and the diffusion rates of both electrons and ions in the plasma are the same. The electrons and ions tend to diffuse together across a magnetic field. However, once the magnetic field strength is smaller than 0.2 T, the β value for the plasma with higher temperature is larger than 1. In the high β region, the expansion of the plasma can still be treated as expansion in the diamagnetic limit where the applied magnetic field is displaced by the field induced due to diamagnetic current [8]. The diamagnetism of plasma plume could be explained as follows. Charges particles (electrons or ions) in the plasma are subjected to the Lorentz force in the presence of magnetic field and therefore gyrate in opposite direction with different Larmor radii depending on their charge, mass and velocity. Due to this the mass of ions is significantly larger than that of electrons, the Larmor radius for ions is greater than the plasma dimension, and the ions can be treated as unmagnetized whereas electrons are trapped by the magnetic field. As the time evolves, ions overshot the electrons resulting from larger Larmor radius and form the positive charged layer at the boundary of the plasma plume, which inducing diamagnetic current decelerates the plasma expansion. The maximum force that induces the above deceleration process appears in a direction perpendicular to the applied magnetic field while there is no any resistive force along the field lines. The above theoretical analysis indicates that the plasma can be confined by applied magnetic field. The experimental results of Harilal et al. and Behera et al. also prove above analysis [2,8].

## 2.2. Enhanced collision of electrons-ions in the presence of magnetic fields

The plasma plume compressed by the confining magnetic field con­ tributes to a great increase in plasma density in its center region leading to increased collisions between the particles within the plasma [24]. The growth rate of an electron avalanche is governed by the diffusion rate of electrons from the laser focal spot. The laser-beam transmission will continue until the plasma density reaches the value nf, which can be expressed as [25]:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

where Dsr and Dsz represent the radial and axial transition diffusion coefficients, which are affected by free electron diffusion and ambipolar diffusion. As the plasma electron density increases, the increased amount of free electron diffusion creates a stronger electric field which also pulls along the heavier positive ions. This phenomenon causes the ambipolar diffusion which is why Dsr and Dsz are related to the ambi­ polar diffusion. Lr and Lz stand for the effective diffusion lengths in the radial and axial directions including the magnetic field effect.

The magnetic field inhibits the loss rate of free diffusion and then increases the value of tf, which contributes to the increase of electron density. A lager electron density leads to larger collision frequencies between electrons-ions. This enhanced collision, in turn, results in an increased number of excited electrons. Based on research by Rockstroh and Mazumder [27] and Bermejo et al. [28], increased electron density in the plasma leads to larger laser absorption ratios and a further in­ crease in its intensity and temperature.

The enhancement in electron temperature in the presence of a magnetic field is due to the two effects: the adiabatic compression and Joule heating effects by the magnetic field [2]. When the expansion of plasma takes place across the magnetic field, heating can occur due to the energy gained by the electrons from the plume's kinetic energy. The magnetic field promotes the electron collisional excitation, which leads to the increase of electron temperature and number density, leading to the increase of the plasma size. In addition to the increase of the tem­ perature of the plasma, the collision frequency of electrons-ions will inversely decrease as given by Eq. (2). This means that there is a limit in the magnetic field enhancement effect of electron-ion collisions in the plasma.

The assumptions for this equation are that 1) all laser radiation energy is transferred into the plasma; 2) energy loss due to collisions is not considered; 3) the energy absorption saturation is not discussed in this equation; 4) energy absorption occurs immediately; 5) the energy absorption rate is the same in all dimensional directions of the plasma. Based on the above analysis, a magnetic field confines the plasma by reducing the diffusion rate of electrons, but inversely, a confined plasma increases the electron density and leads to stronger laser absorption. These two opposite effects will significantly change the size and shape of the plasma.

## 3. Experimental procedure

The details of the experimental process including the experimental setup, experimental design and parameters, the measurement methods and setup for magnetic field assisted plasma manipulation are described in this section.

## 3.1. Experimental setup

A Nd-YVO4 laser (Lumera Lasers Inc.) with an 8 ps pulse duration and 532 nm wavelength laser system was used in the experiments. The experimental setup is shown in Fig. 3 including a 5-axis motion platform with a translation resolution of 10 nm and an ultra-fast gated camera (Model: LaVision PicoStar HR 12). A petri dish with distilled water was placed on the motion platform to generate plasma. A focal spot of 0.85 μm was obtained by a 20 X focusing lens. Rare-earth (Neodymium) permanent magnets (N52) with a surface field of 5000 G were used to create external magnetic fields. The magnetic field distributions were simulated by COMSOL software.

## 3.2. Experimental design and measurements

The evolution of the plasma plume over its life cycle (including its generation, expansion, and diffusion) was captured by the ICCD camera. The capture process of the images of the fluence profile of the plasma consisted of two steps: (1) The plasma fluence (represented by the signal count) was captured by the camera over a gate exposure time of 100 ms (Fig. 4(a)) where each data point represents the average value over the corresponding exposure time in the detection region (Fig. 4(b)). The detection region of interest that contains the plasma, to be referred to as the region of interest (ROI), unless otherwise noted, has a size of 625 pixels; (2) After recording the n th value of the plasma fluence, a delay interval of 8 ps in opening the camera gate is applied to acquire the (n+1) th value of the plasma fluence (Fig. 4(c)). To minimize the laser and background noise, a 532 nm filter and digital noise subtraction were employed as shown in Fig. 3. Besides, the plasma images were saved when the plasma fluence was the largest and stable, which reflects the machining capability under the current processing parameter combinations.

It needs to be pointed out that the characteristics of the plasma im­ ages captured depend on the resolution of the ICCD camera, since the resolution determines the number and threshold values of the photons caught by the camera. This means that the size of the plasma is not its actual size, but the size obtained at the set resolution of the camera. Evidently, a smaller resolution allows one to obtain more data and a larger plasma image size, but a small resolution will also lead to too much interference from the background. So, a resolution of 1 K was selected.

To explore the effects of machining parameters on the shape and fluence of the plasma, single factor experiments with machining pa­ rameters including the repetition frequency of the laser pulse, distance between the laser focus and the water surface (defined as absorption depth), and the direction and strength of the external magnetic field were conducted. The levels and values of the above parameters are listed in Table 1.

## 4. Results and discussion

## 4.1.3. The generation and diffusion of plasma in water

## 4.2.2. Evaluation of plasma size and fluence

The size of the plasma can be evaluated by the semi-major axis (b), semi-minor axis (a) and the area of the ellipse. Based on the equation of the fitted ellipses, the semi-major axes (b) and the semi-minor axes (a) are determined as shown in Fig. 10 and can be applied for the calculation of the area of the plasma. The variation of the above three indicators, as a function of the magnetic field strength, is shown in Fig. 13. Fig. 13 demonstrates that as the strength of the transverse magnetic field in­ creases, the semi-major axis and area of the ellipse linearly increases (consistent with theoretical analysis in Eq. (13)) and reaches a critical point (at 0.15 T), and then slightly decreases. The largest growth of the semi-axis size and area of the ellipse is 21.25% in the semi-minor axis (from 0.861 mm to 1.044 mm), 31.05% in the semi-major axis (from 0.884 mm to 1.159 mm) and 58.97% (from 2.391 mm 2 to 3.802 mm 2 ) in area, respectively, under a magnetic field strength of 0.15 T. The explanation of this is that the transverse magnetic field increases the mean speed of free electrons in the plasma plume leading to more electrons breaking through the plasma generation threshold as well as to larger rates of ionization [30]. All the above inducements result in a larger area of the plasma and its semi-axis size. The confinement effect will have a dominant impact on the plasma for very large magnetic field strengths, which will lead to smaller plasma sizes [31]. Besides, the semi-minor axis of the fitted elliptical plasma shows a similar trend under the effect of the magnetic field as the semi-major axis until the magnetic field strength reaches 0.15 T (critical point), and then there is little difference in the semi-minor axis with the increase of magnetic field strength. This is attributed to the fact that the confinement effect of the magnetic field on the plasma mainly concentrates on the direction vertical to the magnetic field lines [11] which is the same direction as the direction of the semi-minor axis as shown in Fig. 11.

<!-- image -->

The fluence of the plasma is another indicator reflecting its size. The effect of the magnetic field strength on signal count (fluence) is dis­ played in Fig. 14 with an ROI size of 450 pixels. There is also a critical point with the largest fluence of the plasma under a 0.15 T magnetic field strength. The effect of the magnetic field on fluence of the plasma is like its effect on the size of the plasma. In general, compared with a magnetic field strength of 0 T, a magnetic field always increases the plasma fluence, semi-axis size and the area of the fitted elliptical plasma. This can be explained by the fact that on the one hand, the magnetic field confines the plasma and increases its oscillating frequency. On the other hand, the external magnetic field also increases the mean kinetic energy of free electrons in the plasma plume [2]. The above positive effects lead to a higher temperature and energy density of the plasma [32].

## 4.4. The effect of 2D magnetic field on plasma in water

The effect of a 2D magnetic field including transverse and longitu­ dinal magnetic fields on plasma is explored using the setup shown in Fig. 20. With the increase of the distance between the focal point and the center line, the longitudinal magnetic field strength of the 2D magnetic field becomes lower, while the transverse magnetic field strength be­ comes larger, but the total magnetic field strength is lower. ## 4.4.1. Evaluation of plasma shape

Plasma images as well as the corresponding fitted elliptical plasma in water corresponding to different 2D magnetic fields are displayed in Fig. 21. It is obvious that comparing images obtained in the presence and absence of a magnetic field, the shape of the plasma in water is firstly stretched along the direction of the longitudinal magnetic field lines as shown in Fig. 21(b), (c) and (d) with the increase of the distance be­ tween the focal point and center line. As the distance between the focal point and the center line continues to increase, the shape of the plasma significantly expands in the direction of the transverse magnetic field along with size reduction in the direction of the longitudinal magnetic field as shown in Fig. 21(e), (f), and (g). Finally, the shape of the plasma becomes circular like that without a magnetic field as shown in Fig. 21 (a) and (i). The above variations are attributed to the change in the strength and direction of the 2D magnetic fields with the increase of the distance between focal point and center line.

The variation of eccentricity (e) and rotation angle (θ) of the ellipse under different distances between the focal point and the center line are shown in Fig. 22 to evaluate the change in the shape of the plasma. This is because when the focal point is near the center line, the plasma is mainly affected by the longitudinal magnetic field in the 2D magnetic field, while when the focal point is away from the center line, the plasma is dominated by the transverse magnetic field in the 2D magnetic field. At the distance of 1.2 mm, the total magnetic field strength is very small, excreting little effect on the plasma. Besides, the rotation angle increases firstly and then decreases with the increase of the distance between the focal point and the center line, and this also confirms that the 2D magnetic field leads to an elongated ellipsoidal plasma.

## 4.5.1. The growth percentage of the shape and size of the plasma

To further demonstrate the difference in the impact of different magnetic fields on plasma, the largest growth percentage of five indicators including the semi-minor axis, semi-major axis, eccentricity, deflection angle (between the major axis of the ellipse and x axis as shown in Fig. 11(a)). The signal count under transverse, longitudinal and 2D magnetic fields are calculated in comparison to the case with no magnetic field and shown in Fig. 25. It can be observed that the longi­ tudinal magnetic field leads to a larger growth in all the above indicators except in the deflection angle. This indicates that longitudinal magnetic field results in a more significant effect on the geometric shape and size of the plasma in water as compared to the transverse magnetic field. Although the largest growth percentage of eccentricity under a trans­ verse magnetic field is slightly larger than that under a longitudinal magnetic field, the eccentricity value also indicates that longitudinal magnetic field shows greater ability (25.49%) in geometric size change of the plasma. This is because the longitudinal magnetic field line is aligned with the direction of the laser path, which contributes to more energy absorption and a more pronounced magnetized plasma effect compared to the transverse magnetic field. Lager deflection angles are obtained in a transverse magnetic field due to the fact that the major axis of the plasma changes from the y- to the x-axis (same direction as the magnetic field line). The deflection angle under longitudinal magnetic fields is the smallest because the major axis of the plasma is aligned along the y-axis with or without a longitudinal magnetic field. The variation of the above five indicators of the plasma under a 2D magnetic field is the synthetic action of the transverse and longitudinal magnetic fields, which leads to smaller differences between the semi-minor and semi-major axes of the plasma.

Based on above analysis, an ellipsoidal plasma with its major axis aligned with the magnetic field direction is produced in the presence of a magnetic field, compared to a spherical plasma in the absence of a magnetic field. The transverse magnetic field forms an ellipsoidal plasma with its major axis perpendicular to laser field direction. Plasma of this shape possesses the ability of machining wider and deeper channels in LIPMM. Longitudinal magnetic fields produce a larger sized ellipsoidal plasma with its major axis parallel to the laser field direction, resulting in the ability to produce narrower and deeper channels (larger aspect ratios) in LIPMM, compared to a transverse magnetic field. Moreover, the 2D magnetic field has the potential to generate spherical plasma of larger size when the strengths of the longitudinal and trans­ verse magnetic fields is in the proper range. The results described in this section relating to the growth percentage of plasma size and change in the shape of the plasma offers a conclusive proof of the effect of mag­ netic field on plasma shape and size.

## 5. Conclusions

- (1) Higher repetition frequencies and proper absorption distance (0.7 mm in this study) away from the water surface can produce a larger size and fluence of the plasma in MC-LIPMM.
- (2) Larger size of and ellipsoidal plasma with its major axis aligned with the magnetic field direction can be obtained in a transverse magnetic field assisted LIPMM compared to spherical plasma in
3. the absence of a magnetic field. The eccentricity of the elliptic plasma shows a parabolic while the area of the fitted ellipse a linear growth with the increase of the transverse magnetic field strength. The observed maximum growth of 124.85% in eccen­ tricity and 58.97% in area, show the same trend as the theoretical analysis. The variation in deflection angle of the elliptic plasma proves the generation of ellipsoidal plasma under a transverse magnetic field. Its maximum variation is 97.49% when the magnetic field strength is 0.3 T.
- (3) More elongated and larger area of plasma is generated in a lon­ gitudinal magnetic field assisted LIPMM compared to a transverse magnetic field, which show stronger ability in changing its geo­ metric size and shape. More specifically, the maximum growth ratio of eccentricity, area of the fitted ellipse and fluence of the plasma are 111.92%, 86.03%, and 29.98%, respectively. A small variation in the deflection angle indicates that an elongated ellipsoidal plasma is produced in the presence of a longitudinal magnetic field.
- (4) Two-dimensional magnetic fields have the ability of generating large area of and spherical plasma. More specifically, the maximum reduction of eccentricity of the fitted elliptic plasma is 27.04% when the distance from the center line is 0.8 mm, while the maximum increase of the area of the ellipse and fluence of the

- plasma are 12.47% and 16.23%, respectively, when the distance away from the center line is 0.1 mm.
- (5) With the increase of the magnetic field strength, the dimension confinement capacity becomes weaker, while the dimension growth capacity increases firstly and then decreases in a trans­ verse magnetic field. Stronger dimension confinement and growth capacities can be obtained in a longitudinal magnetic field whatever the magnetic field strength is, compared to a transverse magnetic field.

## Abstract

Laser Induced Plasma Micro-Machining (LIPMM) has demonstrated superior micro-machining capabilities as compared to conventional pulsed laser micro-machining. We report a process modification in LIPMM, by which an external unidirectional magnetic field is used to alter the plasma characteristics, which in turn yields a higher material removal rate on 304L steel workpiece, as compared to regular LIPMM. This study indicates that the plasma energy can increase by about 70% by applying a field of 5400 Gauss in either the longitudinal or transverse direction. Correspondingly, the depth of micro-features obtained in the presence of such a field is approximately 50% greater.

Keywords: Laser Induced Plasma Micro-Machining; Magnetic enhancement of plasma

Laser Induced Plasma Micro-Machining (LIPMM) is emerging as a viable and cost-effective alternative to short pulsed (ns, ps) and ultra-short pulsed (fs) laser micromachining processes. LIPMM is an efficient alternative mechanism for material removal as opposed to direct ablation [1] in which the beam is brought to focus inside a transparent liquid dielectric where the workpiece is immersed. Thereafter, by means of optical breakdown, a plasma plume is formed when the peak intensity at the focal spot exceeds the irradiation threshold for plasma formation for the dielectric [1,2]. The plasma, which is an optically opaque, highly localized thermal zone with a peak temperature of 5600 K is then brought in contact with the workpiece to facilitate material removal via vaporization [2-4]. Instead of photo-ablation, the mechanism of material removal is a combined effect of mechanical erosion via the shock wave propagating radially from an expanding plasma, and thermal vaporization of the material in contact with the plasma. This process surpasses the limitations for machining certain materials owing to their optical transmittivity and reflectivity, thereby presenting an opportunity to work with materials having low ablation coefficients, high surface reflectivity and even materials that are transparent to the beam wavelength [5]. Since the effective material removal rate in LIPMM is still limited by the peak power and other beam characteristics, the motivation for this study is to explore a method for improving material removal rates and aspect ratios without an increase in the beam power, but instead by using an external magnetic field to enhance the plasma's energy density. Researchers in the past have reported an increase of up to 50% in the intensity of breakdown plasma in a liquid phase, as a result of an increase in the effective density of the plasma due to its magnetic confinement during the cooling/expansion phase [6,7]. LIPMM using external magnetic field has been reported in the past, primarily to demonstrate a spatial modification of plasma generating un-symmetric features using confined magnetic fields [8,9]. However, this research is focused on exploring the role of unconfined orthogonal

Owing to an external magnetic field there is a net increase in the mean speed of free electrons due to the acceleration from Lorentz forces, leading to an increase in the plasma energy density governed by the mean kinetic energy of free electrons. Based on this hypothesis, an experimental verification of the plasma energy enhancement is presented, by means of measurements through an ultra-fast gated camera and by comparing material removal rates. Moreover, different configurations of the magnetic fields with respect to the direction of propagation of the laser beam have been investigated and compared.

## 1. Experimental setup and methodology

A commercially available Nd-YVO4 laser (Lumera Lasers Inc.) emitting linearly polarized pulses with 8 ps pulse duration operating at its second harmonic (532 nm wavelength) was used for conducting the experiments. The operating pulse repetition frequency was 10 kHz, yielding a maximum pulse energy of 6 lJ after reflection and transmission losses within the beam delivery system. The Gaussian beam (M 2 < 1.2) was brought to focus with a 25 mm focusing lens to a diffraction-limited focus of 10.5 lm spot size (1/e 2 ). The substrate and the focusing lens were mounted on a 5-axis motion stage with a translation resolution of 10 nm and rotational resolution of 10 �4 degrees.

A rare-earth (Neodymium) permanent magnet (N52) with a surface field of 5400 Gauss (both in longitudinal and transverse directions) was used to create external magnetic fields. The plasma was created within four different magnetic field configurations, as shown in Figure 1. Inside the dielectric fluid, the magnetic lines of force were (a) longitudinally upwards, (b) longitudinally downwards, (c) transverse, and (d) absent, corresponding to configurations (a)-(d), respectively. These configurations comprise a comprehensive arrangement of magnetic fields in all orthogonal directions with respect to the direction of propagation of the laser beam.

Figure 1. Magnetic field lines of force generated by bar magnets placed in configurations (a) through (d).

<!-- image -->

Figure 2. Signal count vs. delay plots corresponding to four configurations of magnetic fields as shown in Figure 1.

<!-- image -->

## 2. Results

## 2.1. Imaging

The life-cycle of plasma plume was characterized by an ultra fast-gated camera, and the plasma duration as well as peak intensity was determined for the four configurations depicted in Figure 1. The image sensor was triggered at precisely a few pico-seconds before the onset of plasma, and was exposed to the plasma for about 120 ps. There was also an overall delay of about 17.5 ns between the laser pulse and camera trigger, due to the time takes for transmission over 15 ft long BNC cable. The average signal count

<!-- image -->

(proportional to the plasma intensity) was recorded during this exposure. Subsequently, this process was repeated with delay intervals of 10 ps, to capture the plasma intensities at various instances during its life cycle. The generated plots of signal count are shown in Figure 2, with the four lines corresponding to the configurations in Figure 1.

There is a noticeable difference between the peak intensity and the duration of the plasma plume in the four configurations. For the case of longitudinal fields, in both configurations (a) and (b), the plasma intensity shows a similar peak value and duration for fields along and opposite to the direction of propagation of the beam. For the transverse magnetic field (configuration (c)) the peak intensity was similar to that in the longitudinal configuration, although the plasma duration was reduced by about 10%, which may be attributed to the interference of the orthogonal laser beam with the motion of free electrons within the plasma. Moreover, in the absence of the external magnetic field, the plasma intensity as well as duration was observed to be the lowest. Table 1 summarizes the mean plasma intensities and durations for each configuration.

## 2.2. Machining

Figure 3 shows the cross-section profiles of micro-channels machined by LIPMM in configurations (a)-(d) on 304L steel. For each set of parameters, three data points were measured, and the micro-channel depths and widths along with their variation are shown in Table 1. The trend observed in material removal is in agreement with the imaging results, indicating that longitudinal magnetic fields (in both upward and downward directions) create the most energy dense plasma, followed by the transverse field. Since the material removal is facilitated by a combined effect of thermal vaporization and mechanical erosion, plasma with a higher energy density is expected to yield a higher material removal rate and throughput. As summarized in Table 1, the maximum channel depth obtained for the longitudinal fields was about 50% greater than that obtained in the absence of a magnetic field. Also, the transverse field yielded about 30% greater depth than that in no magnetic field. A similar but less pronounced variation was also observed in the channel width.

These results corroborate that longitudinal fields produce stronger plasma for material removal as compared to a transverse field of the same magnitude. This technique can potentially be applied to achieve greater depth, aspectratio or throughput in micro-machining applications.

## 3. Conclusions

Some key conclusions of this study are:

1. The presence of uni-directional magnetic fields enhances plasma energy density, evident from the peak intensity as well as duration, measured by an ultra-fast gated camera.
2. Longitudinal fields (both along and opposite to the direction of beam propagation) lead to a greater enhancement in plasma energy than transverse fields, as indicated by the difference in measured plasma durations.
3. Material removal properties of magnetically enhanced plasma show a similar trend, after observing the depths and widths of micro-features machined on 304L steel.

This manuscript serves as a proof-of-principle study for magnetic enhancement of laser induced plasma for micro-machining and material removal. This technique can potentially be applied to create high-aspect ratio micro-features with higher throughput, in various materials. However, further analysis is needed to establish the benefit of magnetic enhancement over a wider a range of processing parameters. In the future, a combination of magnetic fields can also be used to enhance or confine laser induced plasma into various shapes and intensities, leading to controlled feature geometries.

## Productivity Enhancement in Laser Induced Plasma Micromachining by altering the Salinity of the Dielectric Media

## Ishan Saxena 1 Kornel Ehmann 2 Jian Cao 3

1,2,3 Dept. Of Mechanical Engineering, Northwestern University

## Abstract

Laser Induced Plasma Micromachining (LIPMM), a recently pioneered micromachining process, offers higher material removal rates and greater aspect-ratios of machined features as compared to laser ablation, while preserving its higher resolution and precision as compared with mechanical (tool-based) micromachining processes. LIPMM involves focusing a pulsed laser beam within a transparent liquid dielectric such as distilled water to induce optical breakdown, and is hence greatly influenced by the dielectric's thermo-electrical properties. This study presents a possibility for process improvement by modifying the dielectric medium composition to target higher material removal rates, aspect ratios and other desirable machining characteristics. We report the influence of salt concentration in distilled water, to achieve greater feature depths and material removal rates in surface micro-machining of Aluminum by the LIPMM process. The key results of this study show up to 100% increase in depth at an optimum salinity of 2-4 g/100 ml. Also, the machining characteristics correlate with the plasma generation thresholds for the corresponding salinities.

Keywords: Micromachining, Laser Induced Plasma, Dielectric, Salinity

## 1. Introduction

Precision micro-texturing over large surfaces has been sought after for various applications like hydrophobicity, bacteria retention, anti-reflective surfaces, friction reduction and other engineered surfaces with desired textures and topography at the micro-scale [1-4]. Many of these applications require multi-material processing, faster processing speeds, and high aspect-ratios. The characteristic sizes of typical micro-features may range from a few microns to sub-millimeter. Short-pulsed and ultra short-pulsed laser ablation is a high-resolution tool-less process for micro-texturing, offering superior resolution, control and precision as compared to mechanical micro-machining as well as other tool-based processes such as micro EDM [5]. However, efficient laser ablation majorly depends on good coupling between the radiation and the material [6], which is based on the selection of wavelength for the material, the reflectivity and absorption coefficient at that wavelength, intensity of radiation reaching the material surface, pulse duration and exposure time [6]. These parameters can significantly control the ablation depth, aspect-ratio and the extent of the heat-affected zones.

Laser Induced Plasma Micro-machining (LIPMM) [7-14] is an efficient alternative mechanism for material removal, as opposed to direct ablation. In LIPMM, the beam is brought to focus inside a transparent liquid dielectric into which the workpiece is immersed. By means of optical breakdown, a plasma plume is formed when the peak intensity at the focal spot exceeds the irradiation threshold for plasma formation. The plasma, which is an opaque, highly localized thermal zone with peak temperature > 5,600 K is then brought in contact with the workpiece to facilitate material removal. Instead of photo-ablation, the mechanism of material removal is a combined effect of mechanical erosion via shock wave propagating radially from an expanding plasma, and thermal vaporization of material in contact with the plasma [15]. This process surpasses the limitations for machining certain materials owing to their optical transmittivity and reflectivity, thereby presenting an opportunity to work with materials having low ablation coefficients, high surface reflectivity and even materials that are transparent to the beam wavelength [7].

Since the effective material removal rate (MRR) in LIPMM is still limited by the peak power and other beam characteristics, the motivation for this study is to explore a method for improving material removal rates and aspect ratios without having to increase the beam power, but instead by altering the dielectric composition via addition of pure NaCl. The proposed modified process would be an efficient, cost-effective and simple alternative to using a higher pulse energy laser, by enhancing the energy density and absorption within the plasma plume, which in turn would lead to higher MRR for the same beam intensity and other beam parameters.

## 2. Background

## 2.1. Dielectric Breakdown

Laser induced optical breakdown of transparent dielectrics has been studied by several researchers in the past [16, 17]. Investigations have been done into determining breakdown thresholds, absorption coefficients and life-cycle of laser induced plasma. The breakdown mechanism plays an important role in determining the machining characteristics, because apart from predicting the plasma intensity, it also governs the beam propagation through the plasma plume. The general rate equation of evolution of free electrons in an irradiated medium can be represented by the following equation:

<!-- image -->

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

Where p is the free electron density in the medium, ηcasc is the coefficient of cascade ionization, g is the rate of diffusion, and ηrec is the coefficient of recombination. Therefore, the terms on the right of equation (1) correspond to the rate contributions due to multiphoton ionization, cascade ionization, electron diffusion outside the plasma, and recombination respectively. Multi-photon absorption takes place when an outer electron absorbs one or more photons to be ejected from its orbit, thereby creating an electron-ion pair. Cascade ionization on the other hand, is the electron-ion pair creation via collision from free electrons which acquire kinetic energy from an incoming photon. In laser induced plasma, for pulse durations greater than 40 fs, the dominant process for electron-ion generation is cascade ionization [18], assuming the presence of seed electrons generated via thermionic effect or presence of impurities. Based on cascade ionization rate, the plasma generation threshold can be approximated by [16]:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

where n is the refractive index of the medium, ω is the angular frequency, ε0 is the permittivity of free space, m and ∆E are the mass and ionization energy of the medium, and c is the speed of light. Moreover, the absorption coefficient (opacity) of the medium influences the fractional intensity reaching the focal volume, as well as the intensity propagating through the breakdown region, governed by equation (3):

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

where I(0) is the unabsorbed intensity, α is the absorption coefficient and I(x) is the intensity after traveling through a distance x (absorption length) in the medium. Therefore, the effective plasma generation threshold is the resultant effect of the rate of ionization, and of the absorption coefficient of the medium.

## 2.2. Influence of Salinity

Due to the availability of constituent Na+ and Cl- ions within a completely dissociated salt solution in distilled water, the effective ionization energy of the medium is reduced, thereby reducing the threshold intensity for plasma generation, and increasing the charge density within the breakdown region. The presence of ions also assists in the multi-photon ionization, which is the dominant mechanism of plasma generation in ultra-short pulses (<100 fs duration), and is an initiator for cascade ionization for longer pulses (>100 fs) [10]. However, dissolved NaCl also influences the attenuation coefficient of the medium, as per the following equation for absorption in solutions, derived from Beer-Lambert's law:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

Where αsw, αw and αs are the absorption coefficients of salt water, pure water and pure salt respectively, and bs is the scattering coefficient of pure salt. It has been found by researchers in the past, that attenuation coefficient has a linear relationship with salinity [19], and most of it is due to the increased scattering rather than increased absorption. Therefore, the overall effect of salinity on plasma generation in a medium is an interplay of reduced ionization energy and increased attenuation coefficient, which suggests an optimum salinity level for achieving the lowest threshold intensity for plasma generation as well as correspondingly greater feature depths and material removal rates in the LIPMM process. In the past, researchers have observed lower plasma generation thresholds for saline (0.9%, or 9 g/litre) water as compared to distilled water, by a difference of about 10-15%, depending on the pulse duration [9]. However, there still needs to be an investigation into the entire range on salinity levels (up to saturation) with respect to their impact on plasma generation threshold and machining capabilities.

## 3. Experimental Setup

## 3.1. Processing Conditions

A commercially available Nd-YVO4 laser (Lumera Lasers Inc.) with 8 ps pulse duration operating at its second harmonic (532 nm wavelength) was used for LIPMM. The operating pulse repetition frequency was varied between 10 kHz and 50 kHz. The maximum pulse energy obtained was 6 μJ after reflection and transmission losses within the beam delivery system, as measured by an external power meter (Gentec Solo 2(R2)). The Gaussian beam (M 2 < 1.2) was brought to focus with a 25 mm triple-element focusing lens to a diffraction-limited focus of 10.5 μm spot size (1/e 2 ). The substrate was mounted on a 5-axis motion stage with a translation resolution of 10 nm and rotational resolution of 0.0001 degrees. A single-pass micro-channel is created when craters machined by consecutive plasma discharges are overlapped by moving the workpiece at a typical feed-rate of 0.4 mm/s.

Commercially pure (99.9%) reagent grade NaCl was dissolved in distilled water by agitation, to create saline solutions with concentrations ranging from 1 g/100 ml to 35 g/100 ml (salt saturation point of pure water at room temperature). The salt content was measured in a 0.0001 g resolution weighing scale prior to addition to 100 ml water. The pulsed laser beam was brought to focus within the dielectric medium, and stable plasma was observed. This plasma plume was brought in contact with the workpiece (also immersed into the dielectric) to machine features via thermal ablation. Figure 1 shows an image of the plasma plume inside the dielectric while it is not in contact with the workpiece. The laser beam was incident from the top of the image into a beaker filled with distilled water, and the workpiece, immersed into the liquid, was kept below the plasma plume.

Fig. 1: CCD image with magnified views of plasma plume (beam incident from the top)

<!-- image -->

## 2.2. Machining Methodology

A 2% beam splitter was mounted coaxially with the laser beam to send a visual feedback into a high resolution CCD camera for monitoring the machining process and to assist in manually translating the substrate vertically to bring the surface near the focus of the laser beam. A two degree of freedom Goniometer stage was used to adjust the horizontal level of the target surface.

For calculating plasma generation thresholds at different salinity levels, the beam was brought into focus 5 mm below the surface of the dielectric, without any workpiece, and the beam average power was reduced manually until the plasma could not be visually detected on the CCD camera (medium was rendered transparent). For machining with LIPMM, the workpiece was immersed into the dielectric medium and brought into contact with plasma plume at focus of beam (see Fig. 2) to machine channels.

Fig. 2: Schematic of the experimental set-up for LIPMM

<!-- image -->

## 2.3 Measurement and Analysis

The depth of micro-channel varies greatly with distance of plasma from the workpiece, which is hard to estimate visually using the coaxially mounted CCD camera. Hence, multiple channels were machined parallel to each other, with different distances of plasma plume from the substrate surface, as shown in Fig. 3 (a). As per the schematic, from left to right, the focal spot was offset vertically up with respect to the surface, to vertically down in the rightmost channel. The step of vertical offset was 50 μm between consecutive channels. This process ensured that the maximum possible depth was achieved was a particular dielectric composition. Thereafter, the deepest channel created was chosen for measurement, as demonstrated in Fig. 3 (b). Post machining, the workpiece was cleaned ultrasonically to eliminate debris. The depth and width of machined channel was measured at three different crosssections and averaged.

Fig. 3: (a) Schematic representation of methodology of micro-channel machining with different locations of plasma with respect to the workpiece surface; (b) Corresponding micro-channels for the case of 2W beam power and 2 g/100 ml salinity (deepest channel is indicated)

<!-- image -->

## 3. Results

## 3.1. Influence on threshold power for plasma generation

It is essential to understand the relationship between the salinity level of dielectric and the threshold peak power required to generate plasma at the focal spot, in order to understand the role of salinity in machining. The threshold average power was determined experimentally for salinity levels varying from 0 to 35 g/100ml (fresh water to saturation salinity at room temperature), and the corresponding peak power was computed from the average power, as per the following relation:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

Where, Ppeak is the peak power, Pavg is the average power, fp is the pulse repetition frequency, tp is the pulse duration and S is the beam cross-section area at focal spot. The experiment sets were repeated for three different pulse repetition frequencies: 10 kHz, 20 kHz and 50 kHz, see Fig. 4. It can be observed that the threshold power was the lowest at a salinity between the range of 2-4 g/100 ml, for all three pulse repetition frequencies. For these experiments, the depth of plasma plume underneath the dielectric surface was kept at a constant value of 5 mm, to ensure same absorption lengths.

Fig. 4: Variation of threshold peak power for plasma generation with salinity level of water

<!-- image -->

As shown in Fig. 5, it was observed that the threshold power was also a function of absorption depth. For four salinity levels, the plasma generation threshold was recorded, and was found to increase with absorption depth. This is owing to the fact that intensity reduces exponentially along the propagation path, according to Eq. (3). Also, the rate of increase of the threshold power was observed to increase with salinity, owing to the increase in the absorption coefficient of saline water. At low absorption lengths, the difference between the threshold power in various cases was within 10%. Therefore, to minimize the threshold, the workpiece would have to be placed closer to the surface of the dielectric.

Fig. 5: Threshold power as a function of absorption depth, for different salinity levels

<!-- image -->

## 3.2. Influence on machined geometry

The influence of salinity on the machined depth and widths of micro-channels is a function of beam power. Typical channels are shown in Fig. 6, for salinity levels of 0 and 2 g/100 ml.

Fig. 6: Depth profiles of micro-channels made by LIPMM in (a) fresh water, and (b) 2 g/100 ml salinity

<!-- image -->

Micro-channel depth was found to increase with increase in salinity, up to 4 g/100 ml, after which the depth steadily reduces for higher salinity levels, see Fig. 7.

Fig. 7: Micro-channel depth as function of beam power, for different salinity levels

<!-- image -->

The maximal improvement (up to 100%) in micro-channel depth was observed at 1.5x threshold intensity, as compared to depths obtained by LIPMM in fresh water. However, at near threshold intensities, the depth improvement was less than 20%.

## 3.2.2 Width

The salinity level had minimum impact on the channel width. The variation in widths measured for different salinity levels was within 5% at threshold intensity, and within 20% at 1.5x threshold intensity with no observable trend, see Fig. 8. This observation strongly suggests that within the focal region, the spatial distribution of energy within the plasma zone is spread more vertically than horizontally. Therefore, the feature width is largely governed by the geometric spot size of the focused beam rather than plasma energy density and strength.

Fig. 8: Micro-channel width as function of beam power, for different salinity levels

<!-- image -->

## 3.2.3 Material removal rate

Since the feed-rate of the process was kept constant and the variation in channel widths was insignificant, material removal rate was largely correlated with the machined depths. To determine the material removal rate, the volume of the machined channel was determined by the 3D volume measurement module within the Alicona infinite focus measurement system, see Fig. 9. The scan area in Fig. 9 (a) represents the portion of the surface which was taken as a reference for computation of ablated volume. Thereafter, the machined volume was divided by the length of the scan segment, in order to obtain the volume of material removed per 100 μm length of microchannel. Finally, the material removal rate was calculated by taking into account the speed of translation to machine the channel (0.4 mm/s). The rates are plotted as a function of salinity, see Fig. 10. Therefore, it would be logical to conclude that the same optimum salinity value (3 g/ 100 ml) correlates to a higher material removal rate. Similar to improvement in depth, there was a 50-100% improvement in material removal rate at approximately 1.5 times the threshold intensity, while the difference is not as pronounced (< 20%) for nearthreshold intensities.

Fig. 9: Volume measurement of 200 μm long segment of micro-channel: (a) Surface image showing scan section, (b) 3-d view of volume measurement, (c) Cross-section view

<!-- image -->

Fig. 10: Material removal rate in micro-channels as a function of salinity in dielectric, for different average beam power

<!-- image -->

The experimental results also indicate that the spatial enhancement of plasma energy due to added salinity in the medium is more along the vertical direction than horizontal, which leads to higher aspect-ratios in micro-structures.

## 4. Conclusions

This paper presents an experimental demonstration of the influence of the presence of salinity of the dielectric medium, on machining characteristics of the LIPMM process. The threshold intensity for plasma generation was determined for different salinity levels. Furthermore, aqueous solutions of different salt concentrations were used to machine microchannels on Aluminum workpieces, and the depths and widths of the channels were measured. The key outcomes in this study are:

1. The lowest threshold intensity for plasma generation was obtained for 2 g/100 ml and 4 g/100 ml salinities.
2. The same salinity concentrations yielded the greatest machined depths of micro-channels.
3. The difference in channel depths was more pronounced (up to 100% increase) for higher energy levels, and less for near-threshold energy levels.
4. The difference in widths was not significant (within 10% range) for salinity levels ranging from 1 g/100 ml to 12 g/100 ml.

This study demonstrates an economically viable enhancement to the recently pioneered LIPMM process, making it more suitable for applications demanding higher aspect-ratio micro-structures and higher processing speeds. However, applying this process modification to a wider range of material processing conditions, a greater experimental and theoretical understanding is required.

## ORIGINAL ARTICLE

## Repulsive magnetic field-assisted laser-induced plasma micromachining for high-quality microfabrication

<!-- image -->

Hongwei Tang 1 & Pei Qiu 1 & Ruixing Cao 1 & Jianlin Zhuang 1 & Shaolin Xu 1

Received: 20 August 2018 /Accepted: 20 January 2019 /Published online: 28 January 2019 # Springer-Verlag London Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2019

## Abstract

Surface micro-/nanostructures are widely used in the fabrication of various functional microsystems. Laser-induced plasma micromachining can greatly improve surface quality in terms of recast layers and thermal defects compared with laser direct writing. Magnetic field has the ability to constrain plasma diffusion and can ensure the stability of laser-induced plasma processing. This paper compares the effects of laser direct-writing processing and laser-induced plasma processing of singlecrystal silicon at the micro-/nanoscale, and emphatically analyzes the material removal mechanism of repulsive magnetic fieldassisted laser-induced plasma micromachining. It is shown that the volume of the laser-induced plasma was constrained under the influence of Lorentz force, a high-quality smooth microgroove without thermal defects was obtained, and its line width was reduced by 30%.

Keywords Micro-/nanofabrication . Laser-inducedplasmamicromachining .Magnetic confinement . Thermal defects

## 1 Introduction

With the development of MEMS and other microsystems technologies, high-efficiency fabrication of high-quality micro-/ nanostructures on various difficult-to-machine materials, such as semiconductors, glass, and ceramics, is extremely important. For example, tailored micro-/nanostructures on the surface of the third-generation semiconductor material can be used to fabricate high-quality pressure sensors [1, 2], microchannels fabricated on the surfaces of SiC are widely used in heat dissipation systems [3], micro-/nanotrenches on glass surface are widely used in microfluidic chips [4, 5], and surface texturing methods on ceramic materials and tool materials are extensively used in friction-reduction applications [6-8].

As one of the most important advanced manufacturing technologies, laser processing method has the advantages of non-contact, precise controllable energy, wide adaptability of materials, and high flexibility, making it widely used in the surface micro-/nanofabrication of various materials [9, 10]. However, laser processing even with femtosecond laser inevitably causes thermal damage, recast areas, and microcracks in the material processing area. These problems seriously affect the application of surface micro-/nanostructures in various microsystems [11, 12].

To reduce the deficiencies brought by the laser thermal effect and the recast layer, some research groups have carried out various studies on auxiliary methods to improve machined surface quality by laser processing. For example, liquid-assisted laser processing has been applied to micro-machining. The presence of liquid can provide better heat dissipation, effectively cool the sample surface, and reduce processing defects caused by thermal damage [13, 14]. However, since the material removal mechanism of liquid-assisted laser processing has not changed substantially, it still leaves thermal defects in the processing area. In order to further reduce thermal defects, other researchers conducted systematic studies on laser-induced plasma micromachining (LIPMM) by using laser-generated plasma instead of laser to physically interact with workpiece [15-19]. The results show that LIPMM is a promising method for reducing thermal damage of machined surfaces.

The material removal mechanism of LIPMM is that the laser-induced plasma absorbs the energy of the laser and then converts it into kinetic and thermal energy to remove the material. When the peak power of the incident ultrashort pulse laser beam exceeds the ionization threshold of the medium solution, laser-induced breakdown (light breakdown) occurs in the focal region, and then plasma is generated [20, 21]. The different mechanisms of laser-induced plasma generation in aqueous media under short-pulse and long-pulse laser irradiation have been analyzed [22]. It is confirmed that the nanosecond pulse laser-induced breakdown is an avalanche breakdown process, while the multiphoton ionization is the main mechanism of plasma formation under the femtosecond pulse laser irradiation. Mason and Goldberg found that magnetic fields can confine the motion of charged particles in laserinduced plasma [23]. Therefore, magnetic field-assisted LIPMM has also been preliminarily carried out with a unidirectional magnetic field [24, 25]. The experimental results show that the external magnetic field can regulate the shape of the plasma and enhance plasma energy density, accordingly changing shapes of the machined area and improving the processing efficiency. However, how to improve the machined surface quality with LIPMM at the micro-/nanoscale has not been well investigated in the previous research.

The research about the confinement of laser-induced plasma under magnetic fields shows that a repulsive magnetic field can significantly constrain the plasma diffusion behavior [26]. Therefore, in this paper, the study on LIPMM with constrained laser-induced plasma under a repulsive magnetic field for high-quality micromachining was firstly carried out. It is expected to provide a way to fabricate high-quality surface with micro-/nanostructures. In order to highlight the processing advantages of the magnetic-confined LIPMM, a comparative study between laser direct writing, liquid-assisted laser processing, LIPMM, and magnetic-confined LIPMM was carried out. The most widely used single-crystal silicon material in semiconductor industry was selected as the processing object. Comprehensive evaluation and analysis of the morphology of fabricated microgrooves were performed. The mechanisms of LIPMM and the process of LIPMM controlled under a repulsion magnetic field were elaborated.

## 2 Experimental setup and design

In this study, an industrial-grade femtosecond laser (SpectraPhysics, Spirit One 1040-8-SHG) was applied. The laser beam was linearly polarized, the repetition frequency is adjustable from 1 Hz to 200 kHz, and the output pulse energy was set at 9.3 μJ. A laser processing system (Newport femtoFBG) with the optical layout as shown in Fig. 1 was used. The optical transmission system controls the average laser power delivered to the sample through a steering mirror M3, a combination of half wave plate (HWP) and glan-laser polarizer (GLP). The processing system is equipped with an ultra-precise three-dimensional micro-displacement platform as shown in Fig. 2. The XY axes each have a travel of 100 mm with a step resolution of 0.05 μm, and the traveling speed can be modulated from 1 μm/s to 300 mm/s; the step resolution at the Z axis is 1 nm and the maximum scanning speed is 2 mm/s, so the relative motion of laser spot and workpiece can be controlled accurately.
