In order to study the influence of the repulsive magnetic field on LIPMM, an experimental device as shown in Fig. 3 was designed on the basis of the LIPMM experimental device. Strong NdFeB permanent magnets, with a length of 40 mm, a width of 20 mm, and a thickness of 2 mm, are mounted on both sides. The magnetic field strength of a single surface field measured by a Gauss meter (CH-1500, CH-Hall Electronic devices) was about 2000 Gs. The medium solution utilized in the LIPMM experiment was ethanol.

The generation of plasma requires a very high peak power density, so it is necessary to use suitable experimental parameters to ensure that the peak power within the micro-sized spot diameter can be higher than 10 12 W/cm 2 . Besides, to ensure the same energy density of laser-induced plasma in this study, the same experimental parameters as shown in Table 1 were used. The laser focus was positioned to about 10 μm above the single-crystal silicon workpiece with the assistance of a coaxial observation system, so as to avoid the induced plasma losing too much kinetic energy in the liquid and failing to remove material. The silicon wafers were treated with ethanol and deionized water respectively for 5 min before and after the experiment to ensure the cleanliness of the surface.

## 3 Results and discussion

## 3.1 Comparison of laser direct writing and laser-induced plasma micromachining

This study adopts a scanning electron microscope (Zeiss Merlin) and an optical microscope (Axio Observer 3, Zeiss) to observe and analyze the surface morphology after laser processing. Firstly, in order to make the processing effect more comparable, the optical microscope was used to measure the machined surfaces. Figure 4 shows the surface morphology after laser direct writing, ethanol-assisted laser direct writing, and LIPMM. It can be found that in the case of ethanolassisted laser processing, the recast layer region can be greatly reduced. However, the light scattering with debris makes the laser irradiation unstable in the solution, resulting in decreased surface quality of discontinuity along the groove's edges as shown in Fig. 4b. Figure 4c shows that surface quality significantly improved with the LIPMM while ensuring that the fabricated groove is straight and smooth.

Table 1 Experimental conditions

Subsequently, in order to evaluate the processing effect, the scanning electron microscope was used to observe the processing area. Figures 5, 6, and 7 show the surface morphology of microgrooves produced by laser direct writing in the air, ethanol-assisted laser direct writing, and LIPMM in ethanol, respectively.

As shown in Fig. 5, when the laser directly processes the material in the air, the width of recast layer caused by redeposition of debris on the machined surface is approximately 6 times of the groove width. Moreover, the laser direct thermal action on the workpiece easily creates hot cracks around the trench (as shown in the red square box) and break-up of large pieces of material (as shown in the blue square box). The yellow circular area shows the phenomenon that the recast layer falls off during the surface cleaning process.

It can be seen from Fig. 6 that the ethanol contributes to the remove of debris and provides better heat dissipation compared to the laser processing in the air, thereby effectively reducing the re-deposition of debris and the heat-affected zone. Some irregular structures appear beyond the processed grooves in the yellow circular area. And as shown in the red square area, the problem of processing discontinuity caused by light scattering with debris in ethanol results in a decreased surface quality of microgrooves.

The machined surface shows different morphology when using LIPMM in ethanol. No debris attaches to the surface outside the processing area, and the hot cracks disappear. Periodic corrugations are observed and become stable at about 600 nm as shown in Fig. 7b. The width of the groove processed by LIPMM is similar to that in the air, which is approximately 16 μm. That is, the laser-induced plasma processing area is comparable to the laser-induced ablation area. Thus, it can be inferred that the distribution of the laserinduced plasma has a relationship with the Gaussian distribution of laser energy.

The surface obtained by LIPMM has a great improvement compared to the direct writing processing in the air or assisted by ethanol. This is because laser-induced plasma micromachining removes material through plasma-matter interaction, which is different from laser photo-decomposition processing and thermal deposition [15-17]. The laser-induced plasma greatly affects the coupling of the incident laser and the plasma in the focal region. It plays an important role in the transmission of incident laser energy. Considering that the laser power density during the experiment reached 10 12 W/ cm 2 , the plasma in this case is a dense and opaque material for the incident laser light, and thus the plasma greatly absorbs the laser energy and converts it into kinetic energy [27]. The front plasma moves at supersonic speeds to form laser-supported detonation wave (LSDW) [28, 29], in which particles moving at high speeds extend to the silicon wafer to remove material as shown in Fig. 8. The velocity of particles from the central area to the outer boundary region gradually decreases due to the Gaussian distribution of the laser energy. Particles with low initial velocity lose kinetic energy during the movement to be insufficient to fully remove the material, resulting in the formation of periodic corrugated structures on the boundary area as shown in Fig. 7. The ripple structure greatly reduces the overall smoothness of the processing area, and its formation is strongly related to the morphology and expansion of the laser-induced plasma. If the diffusion of the plasma can be controlled, the formation of the ripple structure can be effectively suppressed, and the surface quality of the processed region is expected to be greatly improved.

## 3.2 Repulsive magnetic field-assisted LIPMM process

The confinement effect on plasma under a repulsive magnetic field has attracted attention of many researchers. The motion of charged particles of plasma in a magnetic field is constrained by the Lorentz force, thus limiting the free expansion of the plasma [30]. The decrease in expansion volume increases the probability of collision between particles and produces a polarization field [23], which are beneficial for getting high surface quality in material machining processes.

Therefore, the flow of plasma can be limited by the Lorentz force. And, the greater the intensity of the magnetic field, the stronger the plasma is constrained. As the volume of the plasma is compressed, the collision between the electrons and ions in the plasma is also increased. In addition, the electromagnetic interaction between the charged particles of the plasma caused by the confinement of the magnetic field, called as the polarization field effect, also plays a vital role in the focus of the plasma and can greatly change the LIPMM processing effect.

In the magnetic field, the induced electric field E ¼ v-B c generated by the motion of charged particles makes the electric charge accumulated in the boundary, forming the corresponding polarization electric field E ¼ - v-B c . Because of the axial component of the polarized electric field, it presents a certain curvature, that is, the E × B vector has an inner component. At the same time, the displacement velocity of the plasma changes to v ¼ c E-B B 2 , as shown in Fig. 10 [23].

It can be seen that the laser-induced plasma micromachining controlled by the repulsive magnetic field has a great potential for high-quality microfabrication. The confinement effect under Lorentz force, more energetic particles in confined plasma, and the polarization field effect all contribute to the improvement. With a suitable magnetic field configuration, it is hopeful to obtain high-quality microgrooves or other surface structures like microholes, which are expected to be widely used in manufacturing of various microsystems.

## 4 Conclusions

Laser-induced plasma micromachining (LIPMM) is a new type of laser processing method that has the potential to fabricate micro-/nanostructures on the surface of various difficult-to-machine materials. This study has verified that it is feasible to use the repulsive magnetic field-assisted LIPMM to fabricate high-quality surface microstructures, which are useful in manufacturing of different types of microsystems. Based on experimental results and theoretical analysis, conclusions can be summarized as follows.

- (1) Compared with laser direct writing, LIPMM effectively improves the quality of machined single-crystal silicon surfaces. The recast layer and heat-affected zone in the processing area were significantly suppressed.

The laser-induced plasma processing modulated by a repulsive magnetic field takes advantage of the above features, and thus the repulsive magnetic field-assisted LIPMM was carried out with the same laser parameters as shown in Table 1. Figure 11 shows the machined surface topography. Compared with results in Fig. 6, the quality of the surface morphology has been greatly improved. The ripples on the boundary area of groove almost disappear and a much smoother surface was obtained. No thermal defect was observed. The line width decreased by approximately 30% to about 11 μm. - (2) The lateral repulsive magnetic field can effectively regulate the laser-induced plasma processing. The experimental results show that a high-quality smooth surface without thermal defects can be obtained, and the line width of the processed micro-grooves is reduced by 30%.
- (3) The influence of Lorentz force on the motion of charged particles and the electromagnetic interaction between particles under the repulsive magnetic field can be used to reasonably explain the regulation mechanism of magnetic field on LIPMM.

Laser micromachining has emerged as one of the important manufacturing processes for the fabrication of products incorporating micro-scale features and surface structures. Ultra-short pulsed lasers i.e., femto- and pico-second lasers are able to produce high-quality micro-structures with little or no HAZ in comparison to other laser-based processes [7].

A modification to the conventional laser manufacturing process has been proposed by Pallav and Ehmann called 'Laser-Induced Plasma Micro-Machining (LIPMM)' that limits the thermal damage by using an ultra-short laser [8, 9]. In this process, a pulsed laser beam is focused down to a tight spot within a transparent dielectric fluid. The optical breakdown of the fluid occurs if the irradiance is greater than the breakdown threshold and a localized plasma is created. This plasma is brought into contact with the workpiece and the material is removed [8, 9]. Since the plasma, instead of the laser beam, comes in contact with the workpiece, the bond breaking involves photo-thermal instead of the photo-chemical processes. The outcome is a higher material removal efficiency [10 - 12]. The LIPMM process also results in less thermal damage and HAZ because the dielectric fluid can carry away the excessive heat generated during ablation [13].

This paper deals with a comparative investigation of microchannel fabrication using the conventional direct ablation process and the LIPMM process. Ti-6Al-4V, a difficult-tomachine metal, is chosen to compare the fabrication capability of the two processes. The paper discusses the effect of the feed rate, repetition rate of the laser and the number of laser passes on the characteristics of the micro-channels.

## 2. Experimental Setup and Procedure

An Nd-YVO4 pulsed laser system, shown in Fig. 1(a), with an 8 ps pulse duration operating at its second harmonic of 532 nm wavelength was used. The laser has a TEM00 Gaussian power profile which generates an average beam power of 0.08 W at a 10 kHz pulse repetition frequency. A 25 mm focusing lens was used to bring the beam to a diffraction-limited focus spot size of 10.5 ∝m. The Ti-6Al-4V substrate was placed in a Petri dish and mounted on a 5 degrees-of-freedom highprecision Aerotech motion stage which has a resolution of 10 nm as shown in Fig. 1(b). Distilled water was used as the dielectric in the experiments. The substrate, which is immersed within the dielectric, is placed at the focal point of the laser. Since the laser pulse power is greater than the irradiance threshold intensity for plasma formation for distilled water, the optical breakdown of the water molecules occurs, and plasma is generated. At the location where this plasma touches the substrate, the matter is vaporized.

Two sets of experiments, one using the direct laser ablation and another using the LIPMM process, were conducted. Channels were machined in each of the experiments by translating the workpiece at a given feed rate, varying the pulse repetition rate and the number of laser passes. Three different laser repetition rates were used: 10 kHz, 50 kHz and 100 kHz which correspond to laser powers of 0.08 W, 0.28 W, and 0.55

W respectively. The feed rates ranged from 0.01 to 1.00 mm/s. Upon completion of the experiments, the 3D images of the channels were taken, and their width and depth measured using an Olympus Confocal laser scanning microscope. Five crosssections from each channel were taken to calculate the average depth, width, and aspect ratio.

## 3. Results and Discussions

The content of this section is organized into two sections. Channels generated either in a single or multiple laser passes by laser ablation and the LIPMM processes are presented to facilitate a comparison of the two processes' capabilities.

## 3.1 Single Pass Channels

This section discusses the experimental results obtained for the direct laser ablation and LIPMM of Ti64 alloy for a single laser pass. The most fundamental way of creating a channel is simply by passing the laser once through the workpiece at a specified feed rate. It is important to understand the result of the single laser pass on the workpiece so that its processing implications during multiple laser passes could be better understood.

## 3.2 Multi Pass Channels

The effect of multiple laser passes on the depth, width and aspect ratio of channels machined with the LIPMM and direct ablation process was investigated. The repetition rate was kept constant at 10 kHz at an average measured beam power of 0.08 W. The feed rate of the laser beam was equal to 0.1 mm/s throughout this set of experiments. Two different sets of multi pass experiments were conducted. In the first set, the laser focal point was kept constant for all laser passes while in the second, in an attempt to further increase the aspect ratio of the channels, the focal point was translated down toward the workpiece after each laser pass. The downward translation of the focal point was 5 ∝m after each laser pass for the direct laser ablation and 10 ∝m for LIPMM. The rationale for translating the focal point for twice the amount for LIPMM in comparison to laser ablation is because the depth of the channels generated in a single pass by LIPMM is much larger in comparison to the direct ablation.

## 3.2.2 LIPMM

The results of the multiple laser passes on the machined channels in terms of the depth, width, and aspect ratio of the channels without and with a 10 ∝m focal point translation respectively for the LIPMM are given in Tables 5 and 6. It can be observed from Table 5 that as the number of passes increases, the depth of the channels rapidly increases at first and then the rate of growth slows down. This is because it is difficult for the plasma to penetrate deep into the channel as the depth of the channel increases. The width of the channel, on the other hand, increases in a linear fashion and shows no sign of slowing down. The plasma cannot reach to the bottom of the channel so, instead, it touches the walls and removes material from the wall of the channel. Consequently, one can see in Fig. 6 that the aspect ratio increases at first and then decreases due to the increase in the width of the channels. A cross-sectional profile of a two-pass channel is shown in Fig 10. It can be easily predicted that the aspect ratio would start to decrease when the workpiece is machined at an even higher number of passes.

Cavitation Bubble Removal by Surfactants in Laser-Induced Plasma

Micromachining

Suman Bhandari, Putong Kang, Jihoon Jeong, Jian Cao, Kornel Ehmann 1

Department of Mechanical Engineering, Northwestern University, United States

Abstract

The Laser-Induced Plasma Micromachining (LIPMM) process results in higher material removal

rates, lower heat affected areas, and is less influenced by materials properties in comparison to

direct laser ablation. Despite these improved benefits, cavitation bubbles generated during the

process that reflect, refract, and scatter the laser beam pose a challenge for processing materials

in precision engineering applications. This work reports an effective solution to remove surface

bubbles in LIPMM using surfactants. The force of repulsion between the surfactant molecules

aids the buoyancy force in the bubbles to overcome the surface tension which causes the bubbles

to detach from the surface.

Keywords: LIPMM, Surfactants, Bubbles, Picosecond Laser, Laser Machining

Highlight:

1 Introduction

Ultra-short (pico and femtosecond) laser pulses which significantly reduce the thermal

effects during laser-material interactions are widely used in the micro-manufacturing processes

[1]. Pallav and Ehmann introduced a modification to the conventional laser ablation-based

manufacturing process by using ultra-short laser pulses to generate plasma in a dielectric

[https://www.elsevier.com/open-access/userlicense/1.0/](https://www.elsevier.com/open-access/userlicense/1.0/)

medium that leads to material removal [2]. The novelty in the modified process, termed 'LaserInduced Plasma Micro-Machining' (LIPMM), lies in the material removal mechanism. The material removal mechanism in LIPMM primarily involves the thermal vaporization of the material in contact with the plasma, whereas the material removal mechanism in direct ablation is photo-thermal [3]. The photo-thermal material removal process in direct ablation has three components. At first, the free electrons absorb the photons from the laser beam through the inverse Bremsstrahlung effect [4, 5]. The energy from the free electrons is converted to heat due to the collisions between the free electrons. The heat is then diffused to the lattice through the electron-phonon interaction resulting in the melting and removal of the material [6]. Plasma generation in LIPMM takes place due to the optical breakdown of the dielectric through multiphoton and cascade ionization of the dielectric medium. A detailed description can be found in the works of Kennedy [7] and Noack et. al. [8]. As the plasma temperature is much higher (>6,000 K) than the melting point of the Ti-6Al-4V, the material is instantly vaporized [9]. Therefore, the LIPMM process has the capability to machine materials with low photoabsorptivity, high surface reflectivity as well as transparent materials because plasma is the medium of material removal. Furthermore, process enhancement methods for LIPMM using optical manipulation of the plasma [10] and magnetic fields were also explored [11]. This latter process, named 'Magnetically Controlled Laser-Induced Plasma Micro- Machining' (MCLIPMM), has been reported to cause an increase in the plasma energy density and results in higher aspect ratio features/channels as compared to the features machined with LIPMM and conventional laser ablation [12]. The LIPMM process also provides a higher material removal rate and lower heat affected areas as the material removal mechanism is through plasma-material interaction in comparison to the direct laser ablation [13].

Despite the benefits that LIPMM offers over the conventional laser ablation process, its wider pragmatic adoptions are limited because of the bubble interference issue. The obstruction of the laser caused by cavitation bubbles generated during the LIPMM process is one of the most important problems that must be addressed before the process becomes fully feasible for advanced manufacturing. Zhang et. al. have recently demonstrated that the bubbles on the workpiece surface help create hierarchical micro/ nanostructures [14]. However, they also pointed out that the bubble location, size, mobility, and collapse cannot yet be controlled and that the laser beam reflection, refraction, and scattering caused by these bubbles cannot be manipulated resulting in random and unpredictable ablation. Therefore, the bubbles pose a risk for high quality precision manufacturing. Interestingly, much work has been performed to mitigate the effect of surface bubbles in pool boiling experiments [10, 11]. However, there are very few efforts that address bubble removal from the workpiece surface in LIPMM. While Wang et. al. used flowing water in LIPMM process to remove bubbles suspended in water, their method does not guarantee the removal of the bubbles from the workpiece surface [17]. It is important to note that the threat in precision engineering is predominantly posed by surface bubbles rather than the bubbles suspended in the dielectric. Therefore, the removal of the surface bubbles during the LIPMM process is of utmost importance. In order to avoid the interaction of the laser beam with the cavitation bubbles, van der Linden et. al. used low frequency laser pulses of 1 kHz [18] which is not ideal when high-throughput texturing and machining is necessary.

The answer to overcoming the above-outlined impediments might lie in the application of surfactant solutions whose use in pool boiling experiments resulted in the formation of smaller bubbles and the minimization of their coalescence [15]. This work reports on an approach for the minimization and removal of cavitation bubbles on the workpiece surface using surfactants by chemically modifying the dielectric. It will be shown that the use of surfactants in the dielectric helps to alleviate bubble formation and coalescence in the dielectric and on the workpiece surface. Based on this general idea in this paper initial experimental work on suppression of bubble formation will be reported and shown that, once fully developed, it constitutes a viable approach to be implemented in LIPMM.

## 2 Experimental Setup and Methodology

An Nd:YVO4 picosecond laser generating 8 ps pulses operating at its second harmonic of 532 nm wavelength was used in the experiments. A laser pulse repetition frequency of 10 kHz

was used which resulted in an average beam power of 0.08 W. A beam delivery system guides the laser to a Thorlabs LMH-20X focusing lens resulting in a focal spot size smaller than 10 μm as measured by the knife-edge method using a Thorlabs BP209VIS - dual scanning slit beam profiler. The irradiance of the laser

Fig. 1 Experimental setup of the LIPMM process

<!-- image -->

is calculated to be 1,274 GW/cm 2 (which is higher than the optical breakdown threshold of water estimated to be about 491 GW/cm 2 [19]). Therefore, plasma is formed in the dielectric medium. The laser fluence is calculated to be 10 J/cm 2 . As shown in Fig. 1, a Ti-6Al-4V workpiece was placed in a petri dish on a 5 degrees-of-freedom Aerotech motion stage with a 10 nm resolution. The depth of the dielectric above the workpiece surface was about 8 mm. A total of 5 channels were machined at a spacing of 75 µm by translating the motion stage at a speed of 0.1 mm/s for 10 seconds resulting in 1 mm long channels. Two sets of experiments were performed. In the first set, LIPMM processing was carried out by submerging the workpiece in distilled water while in the second set a surfactant solution (Sodium Dodecyl Sulphate SDS, CAS Number 15121-3) at its critical micelle concentration (CMC) of 2,500 ppm was used instead of distilled water. SDS is a surfactant used in many cleaning products and any possible chemical reaction between the SDS solution and Ti-6Al-4V was not found in the literature. A Chameleon CMLN13S2M CCD camera captured the images of the bubble generation phenomenon from the top view at 18 frames per second (fps). The samples were then cleaned using an ultrasonic cleaner for 10 minutes. Optical and 3D images of the channels were obtained by an Alicona InfiniteFocus G4 imaging system.

## 3 Results and Discussion

The CCD camera images of the top view of the LIPMM processing at the beginning, midway, and the end phases of a channel machining are shown in Fig. 2. As soon as the laser is turned on, cavitation bubbles are generated during the LIPMM processing in distilled water as seen in Fig. 2(a). The bubbles immediately attach to the workpiece surface. The bubbles in front of the plasma plume move away from the direction of the machining by the plasma plume as seen in the middle section of the figure. However, most of the bubbles attach to the surface of the workpiece on either side of the channel. The smallest bubbles were 20 µm in size while the coalescence of small bubbles could result in bubbles as large as 600 µm. These larger bubbles cause an even higher degree of laser obstruction and leave larger patches of the surface areas without or with a lower degree of machining. When the machining of a channel is completed, the majority of the bubbles remain attached to the surface due to the surface tension of the bubbles. They will affect the quality of the subsequent channels or adjacent features to be micromachined. On the other hand, the use of the surfactant solution results in the removal of bubbles from the workpiece surface. Although cavitation bubbles still form during the LIPMM process, as shown in Fig. 3, a repulsive external force (green) applied by the hydrophilic heads of the surfactant molecules is now added to the previously existing buoyancy force of the bubbles (blue), and the surface tension force (red). The surface tension force is proportional to σR where σ is the surface tension of the fluid and R is the radius of the spherical bubble and the buoyancy force is proportional to R 3 [15]. The value of σ is reduced by the surfactants, therefore the surface tension force is decreased. The force of repulsion due to the hydrophilic heads of the surfactant molecules also leads to the reduction in the size of the bubbles. The largest bubbles in distilled water were about 600 µm whereas in the surfactant solution less than 80 µm in diameter. Laplace's law for a spherical membrane dictates that the surface tension of a bubble is proportional to the radius of the bubble. As the size of the bubbles remains small due to the surfactant molecules, the buoyancy force is also reduced. However, the presence of the external force applied by the repulsion of the hydrophilic heads of the surfactants molecules helps to overcome the surface tension force as shown in Fig. 3. This results in the rise and collapse of the bubbles from the surface of the workpiece. It can be seen from Fig. 2(b) that at the end of the machining of the channels, no bubbles remain attached to the workpiece surface. Additional research is needed to determine the bubble collapse phenomena and the required surfactant solution and concentration for optimal result during machining, which is not the scope of this paper.

The optical images of the workpiece surface after LIPMM processing in distilled water and the surfactant solution are shown at the top of Fig. 4. The channels machined in distilled water clearly show large regions of no machining whatsoever. After the first channel is machined, numerous bubbles remain attached on both sides of the channels. Therefore, the laser beam is blocked, and inconsistent machining results after the first channel. Conversely, the channels processed in the surfactant solution are not affected by the cavitation bubbles. None of the bubbles remain on the workpiece surface after the completion of each channel. Therefore, each successive channel can be machined without interference by the surface bubbles generated by previous channels. The cross-sectional depth profiles of the channels shown at the bottom of Fig. 4 further confirm this observation. The mid-sections of the second to fifth channels in distilled water are barely machined. In contrast, the channels machined in the SDS solution show good consistency in depth across the entire channel length. Therefore, the limitation of single-track surface processing in the state-of-the-art LIPMM process can be overcome by using the SDS solution.

Ongoing efforts include in-depth research on assessing the effects of anionic, cationic, and non-ionic surfactant solutions at different concentrations on micromachining for a comprehensive understanding of the influence of surfactants in the LIPMM process. The theoretical analysis of the dynamics of bubble formation is also being pursued.

## 4 Conclusions

A promising and effective way to remove bubbles from the workpiece surface during the LIPMM process is presented. The use of a SDS surfactant solution at CMC helped to completely remove bubbles from the surface of the workpiece. The buoyancy and the force of repulsion due to the hydrophilic heads of the surfactant molecules overcome the surface tension and cause the bubbles to rise from the surface in the dielectric solution. This discovery moves the LIPMM process a step closer to be viable in the advanced micro-manufacturing realm.

## Fabrication and droplet impact performance of superhydrophobic Ti6Al4V surface by laser induced plasma micro-machining

<!-- image -->

Zhen Zhang a,b,* , Denghua Liu a , Yi Zhang a , Tao Xue a,* , Yu Huang c , Guojun Zhang c

<!-- image -->

- a School of Aerospace Engineering, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, Hubei 430074, China

## A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: Wettability Superhydrophobic Laser-induced plasma micro-machining Impact behavior Ti6Al4V

## 1. Introduction

Biological organisms in nature have a variety of characteristics, including biological surface wettability like superhydrophobicity and low adhesion on the surface of the lotus leaf [1]. When the lotus leaf has a certain angle of inclination, the droplet rolls, mainly from the special micro-nano structure on the surface [2,3]. The special structure of cormorant bird feathers has good hydrophobicity, ensuring less wetting after entering the water, mainly from the air layer constructed on the surface of the feather structure, so that the liquid cannot directly infil­ trate the interior [4]. Usually, the superhydrophobic surface is defined as the contact angleθCA >150◦ [5], and the hysteresis contact angleθCAH < 10◦ [6].

## A B S T R A C T

Titanium alloy Ti6Al4V super-hydrophobic surface plays a key role in enhancing the water repellency and anticondensation of the fuselage. In this study, laser-induced plasma micromachining (LIPMM) is used for processing an array of cone-shaped protrusions on the surface with a micro-nano hierarchical structure. The relationship between surface wettability, micro-nano structure, and surface chemical composition was studied, meanwhile, the droplet impact behavior was experimented and simulated. The study found that with the aging treatment surface C element distribution and content increased significantly, and the wettability changed from super­ hydrophilic to hydrophobic. As the scan line spacing (50, 40, 30 μm) decreases, the contact angle increased and the hysteresis contact angle decreased. At 50 times and 30 μm line spacing, the contact angle 151.209◦>150◦ , and the hysteresis contact angle 2.619◦<10◦ . The collision experiments reveal that with the increase of the collision velocity (0.44 m/s to 0.98 m/s), the spreading diameter and the rebound height increases. The comparative results of experiments and simulations of collisions present that as the contact angle increases, the spreading diameter decreases, and the rebound height increases. Therefore, the LIPMM is feasible for the fabrication of a superhydrophobic surface and has a wide range of application prospects such as waterproofing, anti-fouling, and anti-icing.

A more complete Cassie-Baxter model [9] describes the case where the solid-liquid-gas three-phase and the solid-liquid contact area fraction f are considered. At this time, the droplets did not infiltrate the internal surface but only stayed on the periphery of the micro­ structure, as shown in Fig. S1(b) of the Supporting Information (SI). Combining Young's, Wenzel, and Cassie-Baxter wetting models, it can be seen that the surface wettability is mainly determined by the solid­ -liquid-gas surface tension, the surface microstructure, and the air layer stored between the droplet and the surface.

Through long-term research, scholars have not only made detailed observations on the wetting characteristics of animals and plants but also extensively studied the wettability theory. Such as Young's model [7] with an ideal smooth surface, and Wenzel's model [8] with complete Inspired by the lotus leaf and other functional surfaces, a variety of bionic functional surfaces have been developed and used in various fields, such as oil-water separation [10,11], anti-fouling [12], drag reduction [13], anti-fog [14], corrosion resistance [15] and anti-icing [16]. For example, Manoj et al. fabricated a super-hydrophobic sur­ face on the Ti substrate by anodizing method, which has a good decontamination effect [12]. Vercillo et al. used a laser process to

fabricate a superhydrophobic surface on the titanium alloy Ti6Al4V, which reduced the adhesion and icing degree of the supercooled droplet on the aircraft surface, so reduced the impact of the supercooled droplet on the aerodynamics of the aircraft [16].

A variety of superhydrophobic surface preparation processes have been developed by scholars, such as photolithography, EDM, chemical modification, etc. [17,18], but there are defects such as weak applica­ bility of metal materials and complex processes. Laser ablation tech­ nology is a process that can be applied to the preparation of metal superhydrophobic surfaces and has been extensively studied, such as ns laser, water-jet assisted ns laser, and ultrashort pulse laser processes [19-21]. The research shows that the heat-affected zone of traditional long and short pulse lasers is larger, while the processing quality of ps and fs ultra-short pulse laser is better. The direct laser ablation experi­ ments in the air by Adela et al. [22] showed that the fs laser has better surface quality than the ns laser. Stephen et al. [23] found that the ps laser can process smoother walls on glass compared to the ns laser.

To further reduce the heat-affected zone of ultrashort pulse laser processing, LIPMM was first proposed by Pallav and Ehmann [24], which uses ultrashort pulse laser to break down a liquid medium to generate high energy density plasma. The process of removing material in the form of ablation and impact. This process has the advantages of a wide processing range and a small heat-affected zone. The feasibility of LIPMM in the ability to machine micro-features on stainless steel has been demonstrated, with a large surface aspect ratio and small heataffected zones [25]. Compared with ultrashort laser direct ablation, scholars have also conducted extensive research, such as Wang et al. [26] used ps laser-induced plasma micromachining method. Compared with ps laser direct ablation, the structure taper is significantly reduced, and the roundness and quality are significantly improved. Bhandari and Ehmann et al. [27] carried out a different study of laser direct ablation and LIPMM for Ti6Al4V microchannels, and the study showed that LIPMM can process structures with larger aspect ratio and better uniformity.

In traditional laser immersion processing, the focus is generally on the surface of the workpiece, and the material is removed by direct ablation. LIPMM has obvious differences in principle: 1) The focal plane of laser focusing is usually placed tens of micros below the workpiece; 2) The processing effect of the plasma relative to the surface position is different. The processing effect is not obvious when the plasma is closer to the surface. As the plasma moves down, the microchannel depth will reach a maximum [28]; 3) LIPMM needs to adopt low scanning speed and low repetition frequency to reduce the influence of liquid ripples, bubbles, and debris (such as forming unstable plasma, hindering laser propagation, etc.) [29]. In addition, scholars have conducted extensive research on LIPMM, such as Zhang and Ehmann et al. [30] studied the evolution and distribution of the plasma under the magnetic-fieldassisted LIPMM, and investigated the machining characteristics of the magnetic-field-assisted LIPMM [31]. Zhang et al. [32] conducted a comprehensive study of the static and dynamic behavior of bubbles in LIPMM. The study found that the higher the laser frequency, the larger the size of the attached bubbles, which is helpful to understand the relationship between bubble behavior and processing performance when machining hard and brittle materials. In addition, LIPMM was used by Ehmann et al. to construct microstructured surfaces on aluminum that can enhance hydrophobicity [33]. However, there is no systematic study on the feasibility of LIPMM to fabricate super­ hydrophobic surfaces and the effect of process parameters on hydrophobicity.

In this study, LIPMM is used for processing a superhydrophobic surface on Ti6Al4V. The main researches are: 1) the surface morphology characteristics of the cone-shaped protrusions array fabricated by LIPMM; 2) the wettability transition of the surface over time; 3) the mechanism of the wettability of different scan line spacing; 4) the in­ fluence of surface chemical element distribution, content and type changes on surface wettability; 5) the experimental and simulation of droplet collision.

## 2. Materials and methods

## 2.1. Materials

Aerospace titanium alloy material Ti6Al4V (ASTM B265) was used in the experiment. The sample has a length and width of 50*50 mm and a thickness of 4 mm. The surface was mirror-polished by a Metallographic Series metallographic sample polishing machine with a speed of 1400r/ min. The samples were washed with absolute ethanol and deionized water for 20 min before processing. The material parameters are shown in Table 1.

## 2.2. Experimental methods

The ps and fs ultrashort pulse lasers are used in LIPMM, which can generate more than 10 6 W peak power under low pulse energy (<6μj), and generate 10 11 W/cm 2 peak power density after tight focusing [34]. When the density is higher than the ionization threshold of the medium, free electrons are generated by multi-photon ionization and cascade ionization mechanism [35-37]. The evolution rate of free electron density in the medium can be calculated by the formula (1) [38].

where: �dρ dt )mp is the electron generated by multiphoton ionization, η casc ρ is the electron generated by cascade ionization, η casc is the cascade ionization rate, gρ is the diffusion loss of the electron outside the focal distance, g is the electron diffusion loss rate, η rec ρ 2 is the recombination collision loss of electrons, and η rec is the recombination rate of electrons (the empirical value is η rec = 2× 10� 9 cm 3 /s). When the free electron density exceeds 10 20 cm� 3 , it will break down the medium to form a plasma composed of charged particles such as positive and negative ions and electrons, and neutral particles such as atoms and molecules.

Through the energy coupling of incident laser and plasma, the light energy will be converted into the mechanical energy and thermal energy of the plasma, forming a high-temperature (>5600 K), high-ener­ gy-density plasma plume with a certain kinetic energy. The material is removed by the inverse bremsstrahlung effect, mechanical shock, and cavitation [34,39,40]. The high-energy plasma plume will generate shock waves in the medium during the outward expansion [41], so the energy density of the action area is high, and the material is removed when the shock wave stress exceeds the failure threshold of the workpiece.

There is a region of high-pressure gradient near the plasma. After the laser disappears, the medium will be filled into the processing area, which effectively removes the tiny hot-melt area, and avoids the occurrence of more molten areas and debris in direct laser ablation. Due to the Gaussian distribution of the incident laser energy, the plasma energy decreases from the center to the periphery, so the plasma plume ablation ability is different, and periodic corrugated structures at different levels can be obtained [42]. The processing principle of LIPMM is shown in Fig. 1.

## 2.3. Experimental procedure

A special laser processing platform was used for the experiment. The light source is a picosecond pulse solid-state laser. The laser and optical components are installed on the X, Y, and Z three-axis processing plat­ forms. The picosecond laser acts on the sample stage through a focusing lens and contains liquid. Inside the medium container, an array of micronano structures is processed on the surface of the workpiece. In the experiment, the plasma generation, shape, and size were recorded by the ICCD camera at the moment when the plasma flux was the largest and most stable. In this study, the liquid medium was always immersed 2.5 mm of the workpiece surface to ensure the machining accuracy and larger plasma size and flux.

To realize the super­ hydrophobic surface structure, the adjacent pits were overlapped with a specific laser scanning speed and processing path to obtain a single-pass microchannel, and a multi-pass microchannel array was formed by multi-layer processing of the single-pass microchannel. The taper of the micro-nano protrusion is controlled by the scan line spacing. Three sets of different parameter combinations were obtained by controlling the scan line spacing to study the wettability changes of different array microstructures on the surface of titanium alloy processed by the LIPMM under different parameter combinations. The above-mentioned related laser parameters and processing parameters are shown in Table 2. The processing area was 6*6mm. The schematic diagram of the LIPMM is shown in Fig. 2(a), Fig. 2(b) is the processing equipment diagram, and Fig. 2(c) is the variation of plasma size and shape at different repetition rates [30].

In the experiment, the static and dynamic behaviors of the bubbles were observed, and the influence of the bubbles on the processing effect was analyzed. Fig. S2 of the Supporting Information (SI) shows the bubble generation and movement behavior when processing a single channel. It can be seen that the laser moves from right to left, and most of the bubbles rapidly diffuse backward due to the reduction of the pressure at the processing path, as shown in Fig. S2(a)(b)(c) of the Supporting Information (SI) red dotted lines, and eventually float on the surface of the medium at the top right of the channel, as shown in Fig. S2 (d) of the Supporting Information (SI) red dotted line. To reduce the influence of bubbles on processing, the surface of the workpiece is mirror polished to reduce the adhesion of bubbles, so only a small part of bubbles adhere to both sides of the channel, as shown in Fig. S2(b)(d)(e) (f) of the Supporting Information (SI), indicated by the yellow dotted line. Observations show that neither of the two kinds of bubbles has a significant shielding effect on the incident laser. In addition, since LIPMM is a process that removes material by breaking down a liquid medium to generate a high-energy-density plasma, rather than direct laser contact, laser scattering problems are also reduced. Both of them reduce the influence of bubbles on the absorption of laser energy and ensure processing quality.

## 2.4. Measurement of surface characterization

After the workpiece was made into the surface of the array micronano structure by the LIPMM process, the samples were respectively placed in absolute ethanol and deionized water for ultrasonic cleaning for 20 min. The sample was then placed in a dust-free air environment (25℃), and its surface micro-morphology, wettability transition, and surface chemical element distribution, content, and type changes were analyzed in detail. The surface micro-morphology included the use of a scanning electron microscope JSM-7600F produced by JEOL to observe the size, composition, and distribution of the micro-nano structure on the surface. The VK-X200K Laser Scanning Confocal Microscope pro­ duced by KEYENCE of Japan was used to observe the three-dimensional surface topography composition and uniformity. The surface wettability was tested by the SDC-100 contact angle measuring instrument pro­ duced by SINDIN, which used fully automated dripping with a dripping accuracy of 0.01 μL. The sample stage can be moved on the X, Y, and Z three-axis, with an accuracy of 0.1 mm. The experiment used 4 μL deionized water to observe the droplet and measure its contact angle through a 1000fps, 1.3 million pixel industrial CCD camera. Finally, an Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectrometer and the AXIS SUPRA + XPS spectrometer produced by Kratos Corporation of Japan were used to characterize the distribution, content, and type of chemical elements on the surface.

## 2.5. Simulation model

To observe the influence of surface wettability on the contact angle of droplets and the behavior of droplet impact, a simulation model was established to simulate the behavior of droplets. The simulation settings are as follows: Volume of Fluid (VOF) for simulating the interaction of air and droplets, pressure-based solution type, and transient solution. The Viscous Model was Laminar. The left, right, and bottom of the computational domain were all wall boundaries, and the top was the pressure-outlet boundary. Solution Method was a PISO solver for Pressure-Velocity Coupling. To ensure the grid accuracy in the move­ ment of droplets, grid self-adaptation was adopted in the simulation, and the grid was refined at the gas-liquid junction to ensure the calculation accuracy. The adaptive settings are as follows: Method adopted Gradient adaptive, Coarsen threshold, and Refine threshold was 0.001, and the grid density was adaptively adjusted every 20 intervals. The mesh of the simulation model is shown in Fig. 3. The specific simulation parameters are shown in Table 3.

## 3. Results and discussion

## 3.1. Surface topography analysis

Through the previous analysis, the surface hydrophobicity was more affected by the micro-topography, which was specifically manifested in the micro-topography structure composition, array depth, groove spacing, and taper. The composition of the structure is directly deter­ mined by the LIPMM. Under certain laser parameters and scanning speed, different microstructures are determined by the scan line spacing. The groove pitch and the structure taper are mainly controlled by the laser scan line spacing. In this study, the LIPMM process was used to process the array micro-nano structure on the titanium alloy Ti6Al4V. Under the laser parameters set in Table2, the ps pulse laser with a power of 6 W and a repetition frequency of 10 kHz was used to break down the deionized water medium at a scanning speed of v = 1 mm/s to achieve micro-processing. The array surface with specific micro-topography was obtained under the parameter combination of scan line spacing of 30, 40, and 50 μm and scans 50. As shown in Fig. 4, the scanning electron microscope image of the array structure is performed when the scans of 50, the scan line spacing is 30 μm and the size of the micro-nano structure is characterized. From Fig. 4(a), it can be found that the sur­ face was processed with a regular array structure, in which the groove width is standard 30 μm, which has good uniformity. The average groove depth is 72 μm as detected by the subsequent laser confocal microscope.

Due to the particularity of the LIPMM, the high energy density plasma induced by the focused laser has a significant effect on micro­ structure processing. Therefore, the microstructure of the topography is affected by the scan line spacing and the scans, including the sharp cone composition, taper, depth, and uniformity. In Fig. 4, from the top area (b) and the magnified images (c), (d), and (e), a clear micro-level layered structure can be observed. Further magnification of the × 100000, (f) shows that a uniform nano-level layered structure is embedded inside, so a uniform micro-nano-layered structure is formed with a 6 W laser, 10 kHz repetition frequency, 50 scans, and 30 μm scan line spacing. The reason for the appearance of this structure is mainly due to the different energy levels and scales of high-energy-density plasma under LIPMM. The microscopic morphology of the array structure with different den­ sities and scales can be controlled by different scan line spacing. Under the control of 30 μm line spacing, the high-density processing of the sharp cone area can be realized by high-energy-density plasma, and the layered micro-nano structure can be processed by plasmas of different energy levels.

From Fig. 4(b), it can be observed that there is a more obvious and uniform taper structure between the horizontal and vertical grooves. The main reason is that when the line spacing is small, there is a less unprocessed area between the scan lines, so a sharp cone structure with a larger and denser taper can be obtained. According to the foregoing analysis, this structure supported the droplets to exist only on the top layer of the surface microstructure, which conforms to the Cassie-Baxter wetting model, as shown in Fig. S1(b) of the Supporting Information (SI). This facilitates the transition of surface wettability to superhydrophobicity.

In addition, the supportive relationship with the droplet is mainly affected by the taper and depth of the structure. A larger depth can store more air pockets in the groove, and support the droplets on the surface. To further observe the microstructure morphology, the laser confocal microscope was used to observe the array micro-nano structure. As shown in Fig. 5, the microscopic image was obtained when the laser power is 6 W, the repetition frequency is 10 kHz, the scanning speed was v = 1 mm/s, the scans is 50, and the scan line spacing is 30 μm. Observing the taper, depth, and uniformity of the surface structure from Fig. 5(a)(b), it can be seen that LIPMM has high processing quality when processing the array microstructure surface. Through subsequent sur­ face wettability verification, the LIPMM is feasible when processing superhydrophobic surfaces.

Through subsequent research on the scan line spacing, with the in­ crease of the scan line spacing, the nano-layered structure gradually decreases, on the contrary, the micro-spherical structure and the microblock structure increase. The structure and tapered shape controlled by the scan line spacing affect the transition of surface wettability. At this time, deeper grooves can store more air pockets, which affects the transition of surface wettability. In this study, the micro-nano structure was fabricated by combining the 50 scans and the scan line spacing from 30 μm to 50 μm with a step length of 10 μm. After that, the surface contact angle was measured to characterize the wettability transition, and the wettability change with the aging treatment was analyzed in detail, as well as the effect of microscopic morphology on wettability, this part will be described in chapters 3.2 and 3.3.

## 3.2. Wettability characterization analysis

Previous studies have shown that after laser processing of aluminum and stainless steel, the surface wettability will change from hydrophilic to hydrophobic over time, and the specific microstructure composition will further amplify the hydrophobic effect and transform it into superhydrophobicity [43,44]. In this study, similar phenomena exist on the surface of the array micro-nano structure processed by LIPMM. In the beginning, the processed area is superhydrophilic. As the storage time is prolonged, the wettability gradually changes to hydrophobicity. For the microstructure under certain parameters, the surface wettability can even be transformed into superhydrophobicity.

For the surface of the unprocessed Ti6Al4V, the surface contact angle was measured asθCA = 87.533◦ , as shown in Fig. 6(a). Continue adding/ extracting droplets, the surface contact angle remained unchanged, indicating that the droplet contact angle, in this case, belongs to the Wenzel model, as formula (2) shows [8]:

where θ* is the apparent droplet contact angle of the curved surface, r is the surface roughness factor, and θ is the contact angle of an ideally smooth surface. In this case, the contact between the droplet and the surface during the infiltration process continues to increase until full contact. After processing with the above process parameters, the sam­ ples were sequentially placed in absolute ethanol and deionized water for ultrasonic cleaning for 20 min and dried indust-free air for 12 h. Then 4 μL of deionized water was quickly infiltrated after contacting the surface with a contact angle measuring instrument, the contact angleθCA = 4.010 < 5◦ , indicating that the initial processing surface is super­ hydrophilic, as shown in Fig. 6(b).

After that, the workpiece was placed in a dust-free air environment, and the change in surface wettability was observed every 3 days, which was specifically characterized as the contact angle. Fig. 7 shows the change in the surface contact angle of the array micro-nano structure from 3 days to 54 days after processing. It can be seen that for the aforementioned laser and process parameters, 4 μL of deionized water was used to measure the surface contact angle. As time goes by, the surface wettability gradually changed from the initial superhydrophilic to hydrophilic, hydrophobic, and finally, to superhydrophobic, the contact angle θCA can reach 151.209◦ .

For the above-mentioned microstructured surface, to further verify the superhydrophobicity of the surface, the hysteresis contact angle of the surface droplets was measured. As shown in Fig. 8, the droplets were gradually added/withdrawn to 4 μL droplets in steps of 0.1 μL, and the contact angle was measured when the droplets just expanded outward/ contracted inwardly. When the droplet volume reaches 4.5 μL, the advancing contact angle θA is 151.189◦ when it just expands. When the droplet shrinks to 3 μL, the receding contact angle θR is 148.570◦ when it just moves, and then the two are subtracted to get the hysteresis contact angleθCAH = 2.619◦<10◦ , indicating that it has a low surface hysteresis. The hysteresis contact angle also indicates that the microstructured surface obtained under the parameters of 50 scans and 30 μm line spacing has good superhydrophobicity.

where θ* is the apparent droplet contact angle of the curved surface, f is the fraction of solid-liquid contact area, and θ is the contact angle of an ideally smooth surface. After the droplet contacts the surface, more air is stored between the surface microstructure and the droplet. When the airbag structure is formed, the droplet is supported to stay on the top of the surface microstructure, as shown in Fig. S1(b) of the Supporting Information (SI). The droplet is supported on the surface of the CassieBaxter model microstructure by the hierarchical micro-nano structure and the air-supported between the grooves to enhance the hydrophobicity.

## 3.3. Effect of process parameters on surface wettability over time

This section mainly analyzes the effect of different microstructures on surface wettability. The wettability transition mechanism of the surface with special microstructures over time and the effects of different parameters on the surface wettability have been studied. The surface difference of the micro-nano structure is mainly affected by the scan line spacing. Therefore, this section is based on aging treatment to study the influence of scan line spacing on the transition of surface wettability.

To study the influence of scan line spacing on surface wettability, line spacing of 30, 40, and 50 μm, ps pulse laser with parameters 6 W and repetition frequency 10 kHz were set. The deionized water is broken down by the ps pulse laser to generate high energy density plasma, and then undergoes micro-processing, where the scanning speed v =1 mm/s and the number of scans was 50. The change of contact angle with time under different scan line spacing and the degree of contact angle change of different scan line spacing in the same period were observed. Fig. 9 shows the change of the surface contact angle every 3 days from day 3 to day 54, when the sample was placed in a dust-free air environment. It can be observed that as time goes by, the surface contact angles of different scan line spacing have increased significantly, from the initial super-hydrophilicity(θCA＜5◦ ) to the hydrophilicity (θCA＜90◦ ). The hydrophobicity is finally realized(θCA＞90◦ ). In addition, as the scan line spacing decreases, the surface contact angle gradually increases. The maximum contact angle appears on the surface of the microstructure with a minimum scan line spacing of 30 μm and can reach 151.209◦ at 42 days, achieving superhydrophobicity. Therefore, the hydrophobicity of the microstructure surface can be significantly controlled by the scan line spacing, and the hydrophobicity is better achieved as the spacing decreases in the range of 50-30 μm. Based on the analysis of the above results, according to the Cassie-Baxter theory, the droplet straddles multiple array microstructures, and the droplet is supported by the storage airbag between the microstructure and the droplet to stay on the top of the surface. However, as the scan line spacing increases from 30 μm to 50 μm, the contact area between the droplet and the surface groove gap is increased. Therefore, the contact adhesion force between the surface and the droplet is enhanced, so the surface wettability gradually changes in the direction of decreasing the contact angle.

Fig. 8. 4 μL drop on the surface of the array micro-nano structure, (a) advancing contact angle θA and (b) receding contact angle θR.

<!-- image -->

Fig. 9. The surface wettability of different scan line spacing surfaces with the time extension, 30 μm, 40 μm, and 50 μm.

<!-- image -->

In addition, the surface micro-morphology and wettability evolution mechanism obtained by different scan line spacing were further studied. Under the same laser and processing parameters, the microstructure images and the contact angle changes in 54 days at 30, 40, and 50 μm scan line spacing were studied, as shown in Fig. 10. It is observed that the contact angle decreases correspondingly as the scan line spacing increases after 54 days. From the analysis of the surface structure composition, it can be found that with the increase of the scan line spacing, the surface microstructure changes from a micro-nano hierar­ chical layered structure with a 30 μm line spacing, as shown in Fig. 10 (a), to a micro-block structure with a 40 μm line spacing, as shown in Fig. 10(b). When the scan line spacing is further increased to 50 μm, it can be seen from Fig. 10(c) that the area and proportion of the microblock structure are further increased.

In the analysis of different line spacings and microstructures, it is found that according to the Cassie-Baxter theoretical analysis, a 4 μL droplet straddles multiple array microstructures. It is supported by sharp cones, micro-nano hierarchical structures, and air stored between grooves and micro-nano layered structures. When the micro-nano layered structure disappears and transforms into a block-shaped microstructure, the supporting effect of the stored air on the droplet is weakened, so the surface hydrophobicity is significantly reduced.

In summary, the research on the scan line spacing showed that the surface morphology is significantly controlled by it, which affects the surface wettability. In the study of 30, 40, and 50 μm line spacing, the contact angle increased significantly with the decrease of the scan line spacing under the same aging treatment. The contact angle θCA can reach the superhydrophobicity standard ofθCA = 151.209◦ under the parameters of 30 μm line spacing and 50 scans, which shows that it is feasible to process the superhydrophobic surface of Ti6Al4V by LIPMM. Compared with the existing superhydrophobic surface processing tech­ nology, only laser processing was used, even if the water jet or hybrid laser processing was assisted, the surface contact angle θCA can only reach 130◦ at most [20,45-48]. If a superhydrophobic surface of 150◦ was further obtained, chemical treatment or low-temperature an-neal­ ing must be carried out [47,48], as shown in the above five methods of Table 4. However, with LIPMM at a specific scanning speed of v = 1 mm/s, under the parameters of scan line spacing of 30 μm and 50 scans, the contact angle θCA can reach 151.209◦ , and the hysteresis contact angle θCAH can reach 2.619◦ after being placed in dust-free air at day 42. It shows that LIPMM has certain advantages compared to the process method in Table 4 when processing superhydrophobic surfaces without further treatment.

Fig. 10. SEM images of the surface microstructure under different scan line spacing and contact angle changes in 54 days, (a) 30 μm, (b) 40 μm, and (c) 50 μm.

<!-- image -->

The above research shows the wettability of the microstructure surface obtained under different line spacings after aging treatment. The reason is mainly attributed to the different magnification effects of microstructure on wettability. In addition, the wettability of the same microstructure surface undergoes a more obvious change with aging treatment. According to the existing research, the main consideration is caused by the content, distribution, and types of surface elements [47,49,50]. The corresponding research is analyzed in detail in Section 3.4.

## 3.4. Surface composition analysis

In addition to the influence of microstructure morphology on surface wettability, wettability is also greatly affected by changes in surface chemical composition. Among them, air-aging treatment of non-polar carbon and its compound deposition is the main reason for the surface transition from hydrophilic to superhydrophobic [47,49,50]. As time goes by, the surface wettability is affected by the increasing coverage of non-polar carbon and compounds on the surface of the microstructure, changing from hydrophilic to hydrophobic or even superhydrophobic. The non-polar carbon and compounds here mainly come from organics and hydrophobic groups in the air.

To study the influence of surface chemical composition on the wettability transition, the surface of the array micro-nano structure was obtained under v = 1 mm/s, 50 scans, and 30 μm scan line spacing. Initially and after being placed in a dust-free air for 54 days, an energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer EDS and XPS spectrometer were used to detect the distribution of chemical elements on the surface. The detec­ tion area is shown in Fig. 11(a). According to the energy spectrum analysis of Ti, Al, O, and C elements for the Ti6Al4V, it can be found that Ti and Al have distributed in more areas as matrix elements after initial processing, as shown in Fig. 11(b)(c). The O element is also more distributed due to ablation, as shown in Fig. 11(d). However, the dis­ tribution area and content of the C element are less, as shown in Fig. 11 (e). After 54 days, the energy spectrum analysis showed that the C element distribution area was obvious, and obvious structural stratifi­ cation could be found, mainly on the surface of the pointed cone, as shown in Fig. 11(f). For the enlarged area of the sharp cone, it was found that the distribution and content of C on the surface did increase significantly compared with the initial processing, as shown in Fig. 12 It shows that the change in wettability has a certain relationship with the content and distribution of surface C element, that is, with the deposi­ tion of non-polar carbon on the surface, the wettability changes toward the direction of increasing contact angle, which is also consistent with the existing research [47,49,50].

To further describe the influence of surface elements on wettability, in the EDS energy spectrum analysis, the surface element content changes were measured at the beginning of processing and after 54 days of storage. The changes in Ti, Al, O, and C element content are shown in Fig. 13. The upper right corner is the atomic content percentage of the element. It can be found that the content of Ti, Al, and O has changed by ± 25 % compared with the initial, but the content of C has increased by 1350 %, and the atomic content percentage of C has increased from 0.04 % initially to 0.58 % after 54 days. This shows that the transition of surface wettability is closely related to the content of the C element.

From element distribution and content changes in Figs. 11, 12, and 13, it can be seen that the content and distribution of the C element increased significantly after 54 days of storage, while the Ti, Al, and O elements did not change significantly. From the perspective of LIPMM, the initial C element was mainly caused by carbon deposition in the air during processing, and the surface coverage was small. In addition, polar TiO2 was produced on the surface due to ablation at the beginning of processing, and Ti-OH at its end is easy to combine with water mole­ cules, showing hydrophilicity [47,51]. Therefore, the surface has strong hydrophilicity just after processing.

After 54 days, it can be seen from Figs. 11, 12, and 13 that the dis­ tribution and content of carbon are significantly different from the initial processing. More carbon is mainly derived from the deposition of carbon and carbon organic matter in the air [20,52]. After the initial processing, the surface is mainly polar molecules C-O, C--O, and O--CO, all of which promote the hydrophilicity of the surface. With time, the carbon and carbon organic matter deposited on the surface of the air is mainly non-polar molecules such as C-C and C-H, which can promote the surface hydrophobic effect [47,49,50]. As time goes by, the coverage of non-polar carbon on the surface continues to increase [50], which leads to the continuous enhancement and stability of the surface hydrophobicity.

For X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy XPS, on the initial processing surface, C1s, O1s, and Ti2p peaks can be observed with binding energies of 285.55 eV, 531.55 eV, and 459.55, respectively. The relative content of C1s was 68.75 %, and the relative content of Ti2p was 7.99 %, as shown in Fig. 14(a). After 54 days, the relative content of C1s increased to 79.08 % and the relative content of Ti2p decreased to 1.80 %, as shown in Fig. 15(a). The content of C and Ti elements was the same as that in EDS.

In the fine energy spectrum of the C1s peak region, C1s was further divided into C-C(H), C-O, C--O, and O-C--O bond sub-peaks. At the initial surface, the binding energies of C-C(H), C-O, C--O, and OC--O were 284.80 eV, 286.08 eV, 287.40 eV, 288.84 eV, respectively. The relative content of C-C(H) was 48.81 %. The relative contents of C-O, C--O, and O-C--O were 39.34 %, 6.82 %, and 5.03 %, respec­ tively, as shown in Fig. 14(b). After 54 days in the air, the binding en­ ergies of C-C(H), C-O, C--O, and O-C--O bonds on the surface were 284.78 eV, and 285.95 eV, 287.45 eV, 288.80 eV. The relative content of C-C(H) bonds was 54.56 %. The relative contents of C-O, C--O, and O-C--O bonds were 32.09 %, 7.32 %, and 6.03 %, respectively, as shown in Fig. 15(b).

In the fine energy spectrum of O1s, there was obvious O-C--O at the binding energy of 534.64 eV on the initial processing surface, as shown in Fig. 14(c). After 54 days, only part of C-O and C--O existed on the surface, as shown in Fig. 15(c). In the fine energy spectrum of Ti2p, the initial processing surface contained Ti2p3/2 and Ti2p1/2 sub-peaks located on Ti 4+ in TiO2, and Ti2p3/2 and Ti2p1/2 sub-peaks located on Ti 3+ in Ti2O3, as shown in Fig. 14(d). After 54 days, the surface showed only part of Ti2p3/2 and Ti2p1/2 sub-peaks on Ti 4+ in TiO2, as shown in Fig. 15(d), the Ti2p was significantly reduced.

XPS energy spectrum showed that there were many hydrophilic polar bonds O-C--O, C-O, and C--O on the initial surface of LIPMM, as well as oxides such as TiO2 generated on the surface of LIPMM at high temperature, which was a typical high surface energy substance, it is easy to absorb -OH from water dissociation in the air. It is highly hy­ drophilic when attached to TiO2, and the polar Ti-OH groups at the end are easily combined with H2O molecules in the atmosphere [53-55]. So the initially machined surface was highly hydrophilic. With the air aging treatment, the density and coverage of non-polar bonds C-H and C-C in the carbon deposition layer on the surface increased during the adsorption and esterification of carbon-containing organic compounds in the air. The polar bonds C-O, C--O, and O-C--O content decreased [56,57], and the polar Ti-OH groups decreased due to the reaction with organics in the air, so the surface energy was significantly reduced and the surface hydrophobicity was enhanced [51]. The layered micro-nano hierarchical structure surface conforms to the Cassie-Baxter wetting model. The hydrophobicity was further amplified, so the super­ hydrophobic surface was obtained.

## 3.5. Impact behavior

In the droplet impact behavior, the contact angle of the droplet was simulated, and then the impact behavior of the droplet at different collision velocities (0.44 m/s, 0.98 m/s) was experimentally analyzed. Finally, the comparative analysis of experimental and simulation results about droplet impact behavior under different wettability surfaces were carried out. The relevant simulation parameters are described in Section 2.5 Simulation Model.

In the simulation of droplet contact angle, the droplet was placed statically on the surface, the measured value of the contact angle was 85.000◦ , and the error with the experimental value of 87.533◦ was 2.9

%, as shown in Fig. S3 of the Supporting Information (SI).

Since droplet impact behavior is related to surface microstructure and wettability, Weber number We = ρv 2 D0/σ represents the relation­ ship between droplet inertia and surface tension, where v is the collision velocity and D0 is the initial diameter of the droplet, ρ is the droplet density, σ is the droplet surface tension coefficient.

A droplet collision experiment was performed on the surface of 50 scans, scan line spacing 30 μm, and 150◦ contact angle. The impact phenomenon of droplets was observed when the collision velocity was 0.44 m/s and 0.98 m/s. The impact state under 0.44 m/s was simulated, then the spreading and retracting states of the droplet colliding with the surface were analyzed simultaneously with the experiment by observing the simulated volume fraction contour.

In the experiment, the kinetic parameters of the droplet are the height of 1 cm, collision velocity of 0.44 m/s and height of 5 cm, collision velocity of 0.98 m/s. A high-speed camera was used to observe the spreading, retraction, and rebound states of the droplet after colliding with the surface. Including the maximum spreading diameter of the droplet and the maximum height of the rebound. Fig. 16(a) and (b) are experimental observations of the droplet colliding with the sur­ face at 0.44 m/s and 0.98 m/s. In the Fig. 16(a), it can be observed that the droplet reached a maximum spreading diameter of 2.615 mm and bounced off the surface with a maximum bounce height of 2.318 mm after colliding with the surface at 0.44 m/s, showing good water repellency. Since the Weber number We represents the relationship between droplet inertia and surface tension, when the collision velocity increases to 0.98 m/s, as shown in Fig. 16(b), the effect of inertia during the collision is greater than the surface tension, and the inertia of the droplet after colliding with the surface makes the maximum spreading diameter larger. The droplet reached a maximum spreading diameter of 3.716 mm. And because there are more airbags between the surface microstructures, better hydrophobicity, and less friction loss in spreading and retraction, obvious bounce occurred when the retraction degree was the largest. And the droplet bounced off the surface with a maximum rebound height of 4.859 mm.

In addition, the dynamic behavior of the droplet colliding with the microstructure surface was simulated by numerical simulation. Collision experiments were performed on 125◦ and 150◦ surfaces, droplets fell freely from a height of 1 cm, and the motion trends of the droplets were recorded with a CCD camera, as shown in Fig. 17(a)(c). In the impact simulation, the droplet collision velocity was set to 0.44 m/s, simulating dropping from a height of 1 cm. The surface contact angles were set to 125◦ and 150◦ , respectively, and the results are shown in Fig. 17(b)(d).

By observing the experimental and simulation process of droplet impact, the droplet first underwent compression after the collision and then retracted after reaching the maximum spreading diameter. The simulation is similar to the experimental trend. When the surface contact angle was 125◦ , the droplet can only bounce back to form a papillary droplet after retracting, as shown in Fig. 17(a)(b), the maximum spread diameter was 2.739 mm. When the contact angle increased to 150◦ , the surface adhesion during spreading decreased due to the enhanced sur­ face hydrophobicity, and the friction loss decreased. Therefore, as the contact angle increases, the maximum spreading diameter decreases (2.615 mm), and the droplet has enough energy to bounce off the surface (2.318 mm from the surface) during the initial retraction, as shown in Fig. 17(c)(d).

## 4. Conclusions

In this study, LIPMM was used to fabricate the superhydrophobic surface of Ti6Al4V. The relationship between surface wettability and microscopic morphology, chemical composition, and the experimental and simulation of droplet impact were studied. The specific research conclusions are as follows:

- (1). LIPMM was used for processing an array of cone-shaped pro­ trusions on the Ti6Al4V, on which there is a layered hierarchical structure with nano-folds embedded in micro-folds. The high energy density and multi-scale plasma in LIPMM can achieve high-density processing in the sharp cone area, and a micro-nano hierarchical structure can be obtained at 50 scans and 30 μm. After 54 days, the wettability changed from superhydrophilic to hydrophobic, and finally to superhydrophobic. The contact angleθCA = 151.209◦>150◦ , and the hysteresis contact angleθCAH = 2.619◦<10◦ .
- (2). The array microstructure obtained under different scan line spacing has different wettability after aging treatment. The

Fig. 17. Experimental and simulation results of droplet collisions, where (a)(b) are the 125◦ contact angle and (c)(d) are the 150◦ contact angle.

<!-- image -->

horizontal and vertical cross array microstructures were fabri­ cated under the scan line spacing 30/40/50 μm. The results show that the surface obtained by smaller scan line spacing has a better hydrophobic effect because the surface obtained under this parameter has a layered hierarchical structure with nano-folds embedded in micro-folds. Therefore, there is more air stored between the microstructure to support the droplet on the surface, which conforms to the Cassie-Baxter model, so the microstructure has an amplifying effect on the hydrophobicity.

- (3). The surface wettability changes in the direction of increasing the contact angle, which is mainly affected by the surface chemical composition. There are polar TiO2 and polar carbon molecules C-O, C--O, and O-C--O on the initial processing surface, which has strong hydrophilicity. After the aging treatment, a layer of non-polar carbon molecules C-C and C-H are deposited on the surface, which is conducive to the transition of wettability to the high contact angle. In addition, the polar bonds C-O, C--O, OC--O, and the polar Ti-OH groups decreased. Therefore, the content, distribution, and types of surface chemical elements are the key reason for wettability transition.
- (4). In the droplet collision experiments and simulations, as the collision velocity increases (0.44 m/s to 0.98 m/s), since the droplet inertia is greater than the surface tension during the collision, the maximum spreading diameter of the droplet increased from 2.615 mm to 3.716 mm. And because there are more airbags between the surface microstructures, better hy­ drophobicity, and less friction loss in spreading and retraction, obvious bounce occurred when the retraction degree was the largest, and the rebound height increased from 2.318 mm to 4.859 mm. As the surface hydrophobicity increased, the maximum spreading diameter of the droplet after collision decreased, and the initial rebound height increased. When the surface contact angle was 125◦ , the droplet can only bounce back to form a papillary droplet after retracting, the maximum spread diameter was 2.739 mm. When the contact angle increased to 150◦ , the maximum spreading diameter decreased (2.615 mm), and the droplet has enough energy to bounce off the surface (2.318 mm from the surface) during the initial retraction.
